I, Gu Wei, have then personally recorded this with a straightforward pen.
I have titled this work "The Genealogy of Life" and examined it through charts and mirrors.
As for tracing the lineages and conjecturing their meanings,

Although I have not yet conducted a thorough investigation,

hoping that those who have not yet seen them may use this as a standard to resolve doubts through broad faith, and that they may judge others by appropriate analogies.

**Chapter One: Returning to Orthodoxy.** This clarifies that the Buddha is the Great Sage to whom the common and the noble alike turn; that the Two Polarities, the Five Agents, and the Three Powers are insufficient as objects of veneration and reverence. **Chapter Two:
Discerning Delusion.** This clarifies the mutual manifestation of the correct and the heterodox, and how the mad and the wise may successively supplant one another;

by comparing and examining these, one establishes the truth without needing the divination of tortoise shells or mirrors. **Chapter Three: The Virtue of the Buddha.** This concerns the Sovereign Awakening’s regard for the mandate of Heaven, opening the way for salvation according to conditions and responding to those who follow his transformation.

Chapter Four: On the Distinction Between Words and Deeds and the Meaning of the Dharma; The Precious Vehicle Proceeds Alone, Gathering and Delivering Those Lost at the Ford—Those Who Attain Its Path Have Their Minds Illumined and Rise Far Above;

Chapter Five: On the Conduct of the Sangha; Successors to the Holy Lineage, These People Broadly Propagate the Way—Their Name Is Encompassed by the Triple Gem, Truly Corresponding to the Single Refuge;
Chapter Six: On Compassion and Sympathy; That Which Is Most Valued in Life: Cherishing the Body and Prizing Life.

The Grand Chancellor of Shang Questions Confucius on Sageship (I).
The Grand Chancellor of Shang—some say it was the Grand Chancellor of Wu, Taizai Pi—asked Confucius, saying: "Master, who is the sage?"
"Is the Master a sage?
He replied, "I, Qiu, am merely one of broad knowledge and strong memory; I am not a sage."
He asked again,
"Are the three kings sages?
He replied:
"The Three Kings were adept at employing wisdom and valor;
as for their sagehood, it is not something Confucius knows.
He was further asked, 'Were the Five Emperors sages?'"
He replied,
"The Five Emperors were adept at employing benevolence and righteousness;
whether they were sages is something I, Qiu, do not know."
He asked again,
"Were the Three Sovereigns sages?
He replied:
"The Three Sovereigns were adept at utilizing their time;
such sageliness is beyond what I, Qiu, can know.
The Grand Minister was greatly startled and said:
"Then who, you ask, is the sage?
The Master shifted his expression slightly and said,
"I have heard that there is a sage in the west."
Without governing, there is no disorder;
without speaking, they trust him of their own accord;
without transforming them, they act spontaneously.

12. When Emperor Gaozu of Zhou visited Ye and abolished the Buddhist Dharma, the former monk Ren Daolin submitted a memorial requesting the restoration of religious affairs. (Daolin) (10). When Emperor Gaozu of Zhou visited Ye and abolished the Buddhist Dharma, the former monk Ren Daolin submitted a memorial requesting the restoration of religious affairs. On the fourth day of the eleventh month of the sixth year of Jiande of the Zhou dynasty.
The Emperor was presiding over the new palace hall in Ye.
The Grand Secretary Yuwen Ang and the Senior Officer Li Delin collected the petitions submitted by those who had come forward with memorials.
At that time, Ren Dao-lin submitted a memorial on his behalf.
When the Emperor read the memorial, he remarked,
"You are one who possesses both teachings."
"The Venerable One possesses extraordinary eloquence that is particularly difficult to respond to;
you should consider this carefully.

Recently, Fu Yi, relying on his own wickedness and stubbornness, has lightly opened his lips;

thus, the screeching of owls and their foul vapors gradually filled the villages,

yet [the ruler], while ostensibly protecting the Daoist teachings, harbored hatred toward the Buddha and the Sangha.
The mutual resonance between things and categories is the same for both humans and animals.

and the followers of Daodi who harbored malice toward the Master.

they rely on matters of fortune and misfortune,
or feign the delivery of offerings to acquire goods.
Having a slight degree of understanding, I am not to be deceived;
possessing a small measure of faith, how could I fail to respond to an invitation?
I feel ashamed by this solitude and am constantly possessed by envy.
They construct empty fabrications and flowery rhetoric to forcibly humiliate one another;
their insults reach the height of ugliness,
and their curses exhaust the depths of malice.

one who recognizes this destruction should surely deliberate upon sin and merit.
Even if it were to utterly consume everything before one’s eyes, it would not satisfy the heart.
As for the executioners under my command, how could they ever tire of the pleasure of their work?
The Book says:

It has nothing to do with the year of Huan Jing;
nevertheless, mountain mists darken the heavens and turbid currents shroud the earth,
while Wen Zhong performs sacrifices out of the proper order.
Confucius did not condemn him for lacking wisdom;
Ziqin slandered the Sage;
and Zi gave him a reprimand for his slip of the tongue.
The saying that "a blemish on one's speech is difficult to erase, for four horses cannot overtake the tongue" is indeed no empty boast.

The former [sage] refuted the ignorant, while the latter sighed in admiration of the holy; the latter, bowing his traces to respond to the mundane, entrusted his substance to this fragile and precarious world.
Treading upon the loom to transform beings,
they share a lifespan of a hundred years; thus,
the fruit is circumscribed by the cultivation of its cause.
Faith and doubt arise from this;
his lifespan was brief yet his transformation was vast,
which is why Maitreya gave rise to suspicion.
A massive mountain cannot be measured by a scale;
it is like a long life that remains vast and distant.
The profound void cannot be discerned by means of cubits or feet.
As kalpas extend infinitely into the distance,
how could one know that seeking immortality from within a snake’s lair would instead lead to an untimely end?
Wearing a dragon-horn circlet while awaiting elixirs will not yet prolong one's life.
Thus, the cicada and the shrike share the wings of the Peng;
the slow horse competes with the steed for distance.
This is the sixth inferiority of your Way.
7. On the Departure of the Spirit and Return to Quiescence, Different from External Migration and the Return of the Spirit to Quiescence, Part Seven. The External Treatise says:
The day the Lord of the Old was first born was already not like that of ordinary beings.
When one conceals their traces, they must necessarily stand apart from the world.
Thus, when the Westward traveler crossed the shifting sands, his path lay through the Hangu Pass;
the blue ox departed the borders, and purple qi floated across the heavens.
Its beginning and end are unfathomable, and its boundaries are unknown.
Śākyamuni suffered from a grave illness in Śrāvastī and announced his passing at the Twin Sala Trees.
The cremation of coffins and the burning of corpses are identical to the customs of the Hu;
when the breath ceases and the spirit departs, they are no different from ordinary people.
This is the seventh difference regarding those who have passed away.
Regarding the internal process of transition and cessation, there is manifestation and concealment. The internal analogy states:
The Preface says that he entrusted his form to the womb of the Li clan to demonstrate to people the principle of beginning and end.
Is this not precisely the nature of arising and ceasing?
It is exactly as Zhuangzi described when he said that when Lao Dan died, Qin Yi went to offer his condolences.
He was born in Dili and died in Huaili; from beginning to end, his path remains unfathomable—how utterly blind is this!

To first lament his passing and later sigh for his rectitude: when the Great Compassionate One’s transformation is perfected and his virtue is full, the conditions have ceased and the mechanism has failed.
The benevolent boat sank between the two rivers;
the sun of wisdom set beneath the twin trees.
Thus ended the assembly of the six heavens and the eight kingdoms.
The assembly of dharma-companions and noble ones gathered like lightning flashing together and winds rushing forth;
they assembled like clouds piling up and mists coalescing.
The auspicious tooth and miraculous bone manifest supreme blessings in distant lands;
the deep blue hair and crimson nails likewise do so.
Manifesting divine power throughout an unparalleled age,
we know that there is neither coming nor going; thus,
the virtue of its vast salvation is truly sublime.
Neither manifest nor obscure,
the wind of literary brilliance flourishes;
how could this be the same as losing one's way back from Dinghu, leaving only the tomb at Qiaoshan to stand alone?

The drifting sands do not return to the Long Mountains of Fufeng; the empty trees—according to the *Huanglan*, the tomb of the Yellow Emperor is on Mount Qiao, while the tomb of Laozi is in Fufeng. This is the seventh instance of the inferiority of your path.
8. The Distinctive Features of External Sages and Holy Ones. The external treatises state:
"The wondrous features of sages are fundamentally different from those of ordinary people;
they may have eight-colored pupils or double irises."
With eyes like the bends of a river and a mouth like the sea,
a dragon-like countenance and the stride of a crane,
with eyebrows arched like a roof and a wondrous tuft of hair between them.
As for such things as curled hair and green eyes,
these are the natural characteristics of the Yi people;
they have high noses and deep-set eyes.
The ordinary appearance of a bearded man—
how could it be matched by the marvelous marks employed by our Sage?
If one attains this retribution through serving the Buddha, [it is truly extraordinary].
The men and women of China have instead taken on the appearance of barbarians;
this is the eighth difference in their physical characteristics.
Regarding the internal physical characteristics, there are many and few. To illustrate this internally, it is said:
The physical substance of the Sage is impermanent;
he manifests wondrousness according to the circumstances.
Thus, there are sages with the bodies of serpents and the heads of dragons.
The Way was manifest in the Supreme Sovereign;
the Lord with twin pupils and four nipples displayed his virtue in the Middle Ages.
The Duke of Zhou’s returning grip was like but a single hair on a fine steed;
Yu’s ears were level with his shoulders.

This is like a single piece of jade from Mount Kunlun. First, the doubts were resolved; subsequently, one marvels at the correctness [of the teaching]. For the Dharma-body is equal to Suchness (tathatā);
its principle is boundless and transcends all designation.
Its transformative essence arises in response to sentient beings.
His wondrous substance is such that it may be described through names and words;
thus there is the radiance of the white tuft of hair and the dark-blue eyelashes,
and the beauty of the fruit-like lips and flower-like eyes.
The mark of a thousand-spoked wheel,
the distinction of the solar orb and lunar radiance,
and the countenance of non-color and wondrous color.
The essence that possesses both the absence of marks and the presence of marks is present in the Venerable Bakula but lacks the latter;
while it is possessed by a Wheel-Turning King, it is not manifest. As the *Sacca-saṃyukta Sūtra* states:
The nature of the arising of non-form excels all marks.
First is the excellence of merit: the eighty kinds of subtle and excellent adornments of the Buddha-sun body.
It is like all sentient beings of the four modes of birth in a trichiliocosm simultaneously becoming universal monarchs.
Increasing it another hundredfold begins to equal the merit of a single pore of the Tathāgata;
increasing it another hundredfold begins to constitute the merit of one minor mark (lakṣaṇa);
and increasing it another hundredfold begins to constitute the merit of one major mark (vyañjana).
Adding another hundredfold more, one first accomplishes the merit of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*).
Adding another hundredfold more, one first accomplishes the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa-śīrṣa*).
Adding another hundredfold more, one first accomplishes the merit of the conch-like topknot (*śikhā*); when the *ṛṣi* beheld it, he grieved within himself.
Alas for the morning and evening of withered leaves; the Brahmacārin beheld them and was moved to sentiment.
He sighed at the rare encounter with the numinous flower—not only did he tread upon the five and grasp the ten to manifest his excellence.
Regarding the *Mēngqí* (the masked spirit) and the *Duàndǒu* (the severed ear), used to manifest extraordinary features, Cáo Zhī’s *Xiānglùn* (Treatise on Physiognomy) states:
"The face of Confucius was like the *Mēngqí*, and the form of the Duke of Zhou was like the *Duàndǒu*. How could Yang Wén and Yín Miè possibly be compared to such [archetypal] beauties?
Meng Zui and Long Lian competed for beauty;
this is the eighth inferiority of your Way. 9.

Regarding the difference between outward appearance and inner demeanor: the external treatise says: [The ninth point regarding the difference between outward appearance and inner demeanor. The external treatise states:

The ancient teachings on deportment and ritual protocol—prostrating, bowing, yielding, and yielding in greeting; wearing the black head-cloth and yellow robes; holding the ceremonial tablet and trailing the sandals—clearly manifest the archetypal forms.
This was indeed the ancient system of the Middle Kingdom, as the critics have declared.
Daoists originally wore Confucian-style robes, no different from those of the common people.
It was only during the era of Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty that they first began to wear the "crossed robe" (hengbei),
with twenty-four seams to correspond to the twenty-four qi of yin and yang.

These originated from human sentiment and likewise lack canonical authority. The *Shixun* (Explanations of Terms) states: "The *kāṣāya* is worn with the left shoulder covered and the right shoulder bared;
the lower garment is a skirt made from a single width of cloth draped horizontally;
the upper robe is a single panel draped over the shoulder."
With shaven heads and exposed crowns, squatting like dogs or crouching like foxes, they do not participate in human ethics;
this is truly the custom of the Rong and Di barbarians.
How could such physical forms be used to match our majestic deportment?
This is the ninth difference in dress and appearance.
Regarding similarities and differences in internal deportment, an internal analogy states:
"Jade pendants and golden pheasant feathers."
Do not bestow [your gifts] upon the wilds of the woodcutter;
clad in robes of lotus fiber with girdles of calamus,
do not tread upon the royal court.
Therefore, the alms bowl is not something displayed in a spirit temple,
and the dyed robes differ from the garments worn for court audiences;
thus, those who ride upon the Way [should maintain these distinctions].
Some follow the capacities of beings to guide them according to the Way;
those who rely on virtue may instead adapt to the times to instruct the world.
Therefore, by cutting their hair and tattooing their bodies,
Zhongni praised the goodness of Taibo;
he reversed conventional norms to accord with the Way.
The poet praised the beauty of the *dàidì* flower;
how much more so for one who seeks to restore their nature and clarify the spirit, parting from the mundane to tread the path of the sage—
it would never be the case that such a person does not differ in their appearance and attire.
Thus, he caused his robes to be like the immeasurable cords of the field of merit;
his ears were not deluded by the lute and zither,
and his eyes were not dazzled by the colors red and purple.
They do not become intimate with their bodies despite lightness and fatness;
they are not startled by the heartless competition for power.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
An Arhat is a true person.
Neither sound nor form can defile them;
neither honor nor high office can move them.
Why must one wear a helmet of heron feathers or a cap of magpies, binding oneself in self-restraint?
Why grind the teeth and pant with breath while professing the Way?
To climb a tree in search of fish is to distance oneself from them ever further.
"To carve a boat while waiting for the sword—how vulgar!
This is the ninth instance of the inferiority of your Way.
10. "The External Formulation of the Divergence between the Normative and the Contrary" (Waishe guishun yi). The tenth external treatise says:
The Lord of the Old established his model through filial piety and loyalty;
he rescued the world and delivered humanity with the utmost compassion and love.
Therefore, his teachings have been transmitted forever, unchanged by the hundred kings.
The profound influence [of this teaching] has long been spread throughout the ages without deviation;
thus, it serves as a constant model for governing states and households.
As for the Buddhist teachings, they abandon one's kin, which is neither benevolent nor filial.
King Ajātaśatru killed his father yet claimed there was no transgression;
Devadatta shot his brother yet heard no report of having committed a sin.
Using this to guide the common people only serves to further increase their evil.
Using this to model the world, how could it give rise to goodness?
This is the tenth difference between the contrary and the compliant.
Regarding the gradual and sudden aspects within the internal Dharma-gate, there is an internal analogy as follows:
"Righteousness is that which morality deprecates;
ritual arises from the thinning of loyalty and good faith;
and the triviality of benevolence is censured even by a common woman."
Great filial piety resides in being inexhaustible.
Yet, to face one’s parents with a mournful song and a smile violates the decorum of the Central Kingdom.
Striking a basin while at a funeral is not the teaching of the refined world; when Yuan Yang’s mother died,
he leaned against the coffin and sang, yet Confucius did not censure him for assisting at the sacrifice.
Zi Sang died.
Zi Gong went to offer his condolences.
The four disciples looked at one another and laughed.
When Zhuangzi’s wife died, he beat a basin and sang;
thus he taught [the world] filial piety, thereby showing reverence for all those in the world who are fathers.
He taught loyalty.
He reveres those who serve as rulers throughout the world;
his transformative influence extends to the myriad states—
this is the ultimate benevolence of an enlightened sovereign.
Manifested throughout the four seas,
this is truly the great filial piety of the sage-kings.
As the Buddhist scriptures state:
The substance of consciousness transmigrates through the six realms;
there are none who have not been one's parents.
Birth and death, and the transformations within the triple world, are likewise without exception.
Who can distinguish between the hateful and the kin?
It is further said:
ignorance obscures the eye of wisdom.
Coming and going within birth and death,
they travel back and forth performing many deeds,
becoming fathers and sons to one another in turn.
Enemies frequently become friends,
and friends frequently become enemies;
therefore, the śramaṇa abandons the mundane and proceeds toward the Real.
He equalized all classes of beings as his own kin;
renouncing worldly glory, he attained the Way.
Regarding all sentient beings as his own relatives, he practiced a mind of universal rectitude.
The intention of universal kinship is that one should still maintain a spirit of purity and detachment while cherishing deep affection;
the Dharma values equality, which requires distinguishing between the hateful and the beloved.
Is this not delusion?
Competing for power, they neglected their kin; in history and literature, they were clear about worldly affairs.
Qi Huan and Chu Mu are examples of this lineage.
To wish to disparage the sages on such grounds—is this not utterly deluded?

This is the tenth point regarding the inferiority of your doctrine. [End of] the Ninth Admonition, Part Two. In response to the *Nine Delusions Treatise*: 1. Throughout the world, there is no mechanism [for salvation]. 2. The construction of images and stupas. 3. Ritual implements and vestments. 4. Abandoning agriculture for alms-gathering. 5. Teaching that governance is the foundation [of order]. 6. Loyalty and filial piety are not to be contravened. 7. The Three Jewels are not subject to change. 8. Different regions share the same regulations. 9. An aged body is not the Buddha. The Externalist’s Argument states: [End of section].
Now, speech does not prize flowery rhetoric;
it values internal coherence.
Song does not prize clear resonance.
The esteemed materials are harmonized with the rhythm.
In the Buddhist scriptures,
when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma:
The sons of heaven from all lands gathered together to listen.
Some emitted radiance that pervaded the great trichiliocosm.
This was during the time when Śākyamuni was in the world, corresponding to my own Zhou dynasty.
What is recorded in the historical annals is certainly without omission;
yet we have never heard that a Heavenly King traveled to those Onion Mountains (Pamirs).
How could this be fitting for an Emperor of the Central Kingdom?
There is no one who does not participate in the Dharma assembly;
even the rulers of remote borderlands,
if they possess the karmic affinity, shall be universally moistened by the Dharma seat.
Wherever the light shines, sentient beings are freed from suffering;
yet what fault has this land committed that it alone lacks those who awaken?
It remains isolated beyond the reach of grace, never having seen or heard [the teaching].
Looking up to the Compassionate Sage (Nengren), who admits no partiality or simplification, [the Master] rebuked him, saying:

"You have no merit for having seen the Buddha, yet you bear the fault of slandering the Holy One. How can you harbor resentment toward the spirits? You must only blame yourself. When you seek the mind and examine the reality, your actions are at odds and your words are contradictory."
Deceptive falsehoods are so glaringly evident that they are fully worthy of being called hypocrisy;
yet ordinary people fail to awaken to this, merely chasing shadows and barking at sounds,
such that the world remains unaware.
Their delusion is one and the same. 1.
"The Inner World Lacks the Mechanism" (Neizhou shi wuji zhi). The first inner admonition says:
Now, when the Primeval and the Xi were adorned by Heaven...
The blind cannot perceive its color;
when thunder shakes the earth,
the deaf do not hear its sound.
This is because their karmic resonance is utterly severed.
When they act with violence as the most wicked and cruel,
even Confucius’s wisdom could not have restrained their hearts.
When a rustic man is bound by indignation, even if he is granted eloquence, he cannot dispel his resentment;
this is also a divergence in temperament and nature. As Zhuangzi said:
Confucius went to see Robber Zhi.
Robber Zhi, in turn, rebuked Confucius.
Confucius became fearful, hesitated, and withdrew.
Liu Zi said:
"When Confucius's horse grazed upon the crops of a countryman,
the man grew angry and stopped the horse."
Confucius sent Zi Gong to persuade and resolve the matter, but the rustic grew even more enraged.
Confucius then dispatched his horse-herder to deliver his message, whereupon the rustic was pleased.
Thus, when the Way harmonizes, there is a response from ten thousand li away.
When circumstances diverge, even the liver and gallbladder become as distant as Chu and Yue;
how much more so when beginningless bonds have been vast for so long,
and the afflictions of craving are deeper than the blue sea?
The conditioned activities are vast;
the afflictions vie with the great mountains in their loftiness.
The myriad emotions cannot arrive all at once.
Therefore, one guides them through gradual accumulation;
since it is impossible to cultivate all practices simultaneously, one urges them on by means of limited stages.
This is like the three transformations of heaven and earth, which initially merge with the natural state, as Laozi said.
Man models himself on the Earth;
the Earth models itself on Heaven;
Heaven models itself on the Dao. It was only after Qi and Lu underwent a second transformation that they reached the Ultimate Dao.
Dense clouds precede the timely rain;
the solid ice begins with the trampling of frost;
these are all examples of what is called gradual accumulation.
Therefore, regarding the two Sovereigns who presided over the transformation of the four realms of Mount Sumeru, the *Sūtra on the Response to Sound* states:
"The Bodhisattva Yingsheng was Fuxi, and the Bodhisattva Jixiang was Nüwa; they dwelt at the beginning of the Stilling Wind."

Regarding the words established by the Three Sages, the *Kongji Suowen Jing* (Sūtra on the Questions Concerning Emptiness and Stillness) states: "Kāśyapa was Laozi, Rujung was Confucius, and Guangjing was Yán Huí; they appeared at the end of the era of purity."
The principle of profound emptiness and the singular unity was flourishing in the discourse of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi;
the texts of the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music were likewise esteemed.
The Duke of Zhou and Confucius flourished their teachings;
by clarifying humility and maintaining simplicity,
they ascended the阶梯 (staircase) to sagehood.
The three fears and the five constants serve as the gradual path for becoming a human or a celestial being;
they indeed correspond in secret with the principles of the Buddha.
It is not the ultimate discourse of correct debate;
it is like seeking the Way from the mute and the deaf,
waving one's hand toward the four directions while unable to discern distance or proximity.
Inquiring about the ford at the place where the rabbit and horse met,
one knows how to cross but cannot fathom its depth;
it is from this that our discussion proceeds.
The eras of the Yin and Zhou dynasties were not times when the teachings of Śākyamuni ought to have been practiced.
It is like the blazing intensity of the sun's heat:
even a child cannot look directly at it with his eyes.
The thunderbolt strikes with such sudden force that even a weakling cannot open his ears to hear it; thus,
the rivers and ponds surge and overflow.
King Zhao was terrified by the manifestation of spirits;
the clouds and rainbows changed their colors.
Empress Mu rejoiced at the passing of the Sage. The *Zhou Shu Yi Ji* (Record of Marvels from the Book of Zhou) says:

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao’s reign, the rivers, streams, springs, and ponds all overflowed. On the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu’s reign.
A violent wind suddenly arose, breaking and snapping the trees;
the sky grew overcast and the clouds turned black.
With the omen of a white rainbow appearing, how could he have crossed the Pamir Mountains and the Tarim River to receive his transformation?
Crossing the Snowy Range to offer my sincere devotion,
I am reminded of what the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* says:
"This is the fault of the blind, not the fault of the sun and moon."
I was just about to exhaust the arguments regarding the boring out of his apertures,
fearing it might injure your state of primordial unity;
this is not something you can understand.
Their blindness is one and the same.
An external treatise states:
"When the copper mountain collapses, the bronze bell resonates."
When the moon’s halo wanes as the reed-ash clock runs out,
the tiger does not yet roar to stir the wind,
nor does the dragon soar to raise the clouds.
Now, the Buddha-power spoken of by Śākyamuni is most supreme;
with a single thought, he brings his response to wherever the mind is directed.
Therefore, both the common people and the secular elite each exhaust their wealth and property, vying with one another to construct stupas and temples.
Without begrudging pearls or jade, they vied with one another to construct halls and pavilions;
some molded clay or carved sandalwood to depict the features of the Xiongnu.
Casting gold and weaving silk,
they replace the appearance of the barbarians;
the subtlety exhausts the art of painting, and the ingenuity reaches the limit of carving.
With every prostration and every salutation, one hopes for a spiritual resonance.
Since the Dharma of the Hu people gradually spread southward more than six hundred years ago,
I have never heard of a single person claiming to have been able to see the Buddha.
Is it that only when a barbarian prostrates does one encounter the Tathāgata,
while in the land of Han, despite our reverent devotion, we do not meet the Tamer of Men?
If the transformation [of the Dharma] did not reach this place, then it would indeed lack spiritual efficacy.
They deceive and delude people with empty talk of their own powers,
yet the world cannot perceive it;
this is the second kind of delusion.
2. Constructing Images and Stūpas Within: Regarding the construction of images and stūpas within [the body], the second internal admonition states:
"Zuo Che admired the Sage;
he carved an image and prostrated before the Emperor of Xuan."
Goujian longed for the worthy;
he melted gold to cast a mold of a conch shell.
Ding Lan was truly filial.
Carving and engraving serve as a substitute for personal attendance;
the countenance is present through the provision of benevolence,
while colored jade and precious stones depict the Sage.
Thus, it causes sorrow and joy to manifest upon one's countenance and sincere devotion to penetrate even into dreams;
this is indeed the ultimate.
How could it compare to the non-returning [state] of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?
Because of this, King Udayana carved it from wood,
causing the dense forest to darken with its shadow;
and thus, King Ajātaśatru cast it in gold.
The wondrous features were entrusted to brush and ink,
and the numinous countenance was committed to refined metal;
some beheld the true form and withdrew from their seats, while others turned their bodies to capture the likeness, as recorded in the *Ganying zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance).
At Changgan Temple in Yangzhou, there was a statue of King Aśoka that people wished to copy by tracing.
The temple monks, fearing it would damage the gilded surface, did not permit it.
The patron who commissioned the statue then made a sincere vow.
If one prays with sincere devotion, the image will turn its body to face west.
Thereupon, [the chamber] was securely locked at the high pavilion;
when opened for inspection the following morning, the body of the image was found to be facing west as promised. The divine response is inexhaustible, and its origins date back to ancient times.
Since the image itself flowed eastward to receive the True Teaching and the Dharma moved south,
there were dreams at dusk of a golden man and a jade horse floating upon the river;
divine light guided the way across the Xiang River.
Auspicious radiance emanated from the Tanxi [Pond]; as recorded in the *Ganying zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance).
The *Yuwang xiang ji* (Record of the Image of the Buddha of the Universal Monarch) at Fameng Temple in Luling states that the body of the image originated in Luling.
At Sanqu, auspicious light emerged from the pedestal at Zhaotan in Xiangzhou, radiating brilliant light that illuminated the cliffs and banks.
At Tanchi Temple in Wuchang, an auspicious image manifested from within the Tanchi stream.
The radiance reflecting upon the waters reveals the form of the sun rising over Changsha;
the Luoyue Peak manifests the lustrous quality of gold.
These matters are extensive.
To speak briefly: it is as found in works such as Qian Bao’s *Sou Shen Ji* (Search for the Spirits), the *Linchuan Xuan Yan Ji* (Record of Manifested Verifications from Linchuan),

the *Zheng Ying Ming Xiang Ji* (Record of Miraculous Responses and Hidden Auspiciousness), and the *You Ming Lu* (Records of the Hidden and the Visible) and *Gan Ying Zhuan* (Biographies of Responsive Manifestations).
From the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty down to the Qi and Liang dynasties,
there were kings, dukes, governors, and prefects,
as well as laymen and laywomen of pure faith, along with bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Those who, through profound resonance, beheld divine light with their own eyes before the Most Holy One numbered more than two hundred.
As for those who witnessed traces, there were the floating radiance among the myriad mountains and the glow at Hudu.
Beneath the Qingtai Observatory, they beheld the form of the full moon;
outside the Yongmen Gate, they observed the shadow of the *stūpa* spire.
At Nanping, they obtained a response from the auspicious image.
Emperor Wenxuan was moved by a dream concerning Shengya;
Empress Xiao cast it once and completed it,
whereas Emperor Song attempted to mold it four times without success— examples of this kind are numerous.
It cannot be fully recounted.
How could one, on account of your own lack of vision, deny the spiritual nature of that which possesses it?
Nevertheless, there is nothing that its virtue does not encompass.
That which is called nirvana is that wherein the Way has no obstruction;
this is named bodhi.
One whose wisdom is all-pervading is called a Buddha;
this is the Chinese translation of that Sanskrit term.
Thus, the Buddhas of both [this and that world] can be clearly and reliably trusted.
How is this made clear? For the Buddha—
"Bodhi" in the language of Han means "Great Enlightenment.
"Bodhi" in the language of Han means "Great Way."
Nirvana, in the Han language,
means the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Yet you,
my son, spend your whole day treading upon the ground of Bodhi.
One does not realize that the Great Way (Mahāyāna) is but another name for Bodhi.
Having received a physical form within the realm of the Great Awakened One—
wherein "Great Awakened One" (Dàjué) is the translated name for Buddha— one has yet to become proficient in the teachings of the Great Awakened One.
Therefore Zhuang Zhou said:
"Furthermore, it is only after one has attained great awakening that one realizes this was a great dream."
Guo’s Commentary:
The "Awakened One" refers to the Sage.
This means that those who harbor anxieties in their hearts have all not yet attained enlightenment.
"Both you and I are in a dream," he said.
The commentary notes:
"The Master and Ziyou were both unable to transcend words to achieve spiritual understanding."
Therefore, he was not one of great awakening.
The gentleman said:
"Kong Qiu’s discourse on this matter has reached its limit."
Nirvana is quiescent illumination; it cannot be known by consciousness, nor can it be understood by wisdom.
Thus, speech is cut off and the movements of the mind cease;
therefore, one forgets words.
The Dharma-body is constituted by the three points and four virtues;
being serene and free from all entanglements,
it is called liberation.
This is because his spirit was liberated and his afflictions were stilled.
Although the Master was a sage,
he distantly attributed his merit to the Buddha.
According to Liu Xiang’s two ancient catalogs,

Nevertheless, both Zhou and Lao appear together in Buddhist scriptures;

Now, the Yi is characterized by non-action;

I shall now speak to you with my own ears.
You should cast off your long-accumulated delusions and embrace this late awakening.
The tradition of stūpa construction has indeed spread far and wide.

To guide those who are mute or deaf, one must surely bend and look up while pointing and gesturing;
to awaken those who are ignorant or obstructed, one likewise raises the ear and lifts the palm.
For human relations are fundamentally rooted in filial piety and reverence.
Filial piety and reverence are derived from the act of procreation;
thus it is said:
"Without one's parents, one would not be born."
Without sages, there would be no establishment of order;
without sages, there would be no Dharma;
without filial piety, there would be no parents.
Thus, the principle of generation and completion is universal,
and the affection between teacher and disciple is manifest;
hence, when Yan Hui died—
Yan Lu requested the carriage of the Master.
Confucius said,
"Hui regards me as his father, yet I cannot regard him as my son."
This is indeed its underlying meaning.
Furthermore, the ritual expressions of affection and reverence differ in form, yet they do not transcend two principles;
the natures of the wise and the foolish vary in quality, yet they do not exceed three stages.
Therefore, while alive, one provides filial support without fail;
after death, one performs burial and sacrifice according to ritual.
This is the distinction of the ritual system.
In lesser filial piety, one exerts physical strength;
in middling filial piety, one exerts labor;
in great filial piety, there is no depletion.
This is a distinction within the nature [of the teachings].
When compared with the Buddhist teachings, their meaning is contained therein.
As for those who practice such things as sprinkling blood or burning the body—
The ritual of the jeweled stupa and the benevolent shrine is also what is meant by "respecting the beginning and being cautious about the end.
As for the Wheel-Turning King, the Eighty Thousand [Buddhas], the Three Thousand Lords of the Śākyas, and King Aśoka, the *Ayuwang jing* (Sutra of King Aśoka) states:
The king killed eighty-four thousand palace women.
At night, he heard the sound of weeping within the palace.
The king repented and built eighty-four thousand stupas for them.
Now, there are also those who exist here in this land of China.
Śakra-devānām-indra constructed three thousand stūpas in the heavens, exhausting the vast oceans in search of jewels and clearing the pure thoroughfares to transport stones.
This is indeed a laborious task.
To take the welfare of all living beings as one's own responsibility,
and to regard all sentient creatures as equal members of the celestial kinship— this is the essence of the matter.
To dwell in the ruin of the tainted world and to shoulder the burden of those who are incorrigible—
this is indeed a weariness of the mind.
Turning the carriage toward the realm of true reality,
he concentrated his spirit in the field of tranquil illumination;
pointing toward nirvana, he made his eternal return.
Riding upon the Dharma-body to gaze afar—
this is the inexhaustible Way.
It was when his mother descended from heaven that [the lineage] began.
He opened the golden coffin and expounded the verses.
When his father, the King, passed away, he took up the jeweled couch to conduct the funeral rites. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: [as cited above].
When King Śuddhodana passed away,
the Buddha himself took hold of one leg of the corded bier and proceeded to the site of cremation. Thus,

for all sentient beings of future generations, he fully demonstrated how to repay the kindness of those who gave birth and nurtured them, and how to manifest the outward forms of filial piety and reverence.
From where did the teaching to discard the remains come?
Furthermore, the sutras encourage the universal offering of corpses to flying and crawling creatures;
this intention lies in settling past debts in hopes of escaping future retribution.
It is not as Zhuang Zhou claimed— that elaborate funerals in the final age are the root of lost ritual propriety—
yet he asked why ants should be considered kin while birds and beasts are considered distant.
Since life is already like staying at an inn for this body, [how can one cling to it?]
Upon death, one should take heaven and earth as the outer and inner coffins.
This returns to the ancient practice of not permitting burial, which avoids the detestable matter [of the grave].
It is a remedy for the弊 (evil/defect) of slighting life and valuing death.

Those who seek the Way of the Immortals may carry their books on bamboo frames to follow teachers, or shoulder their staffs to travel to distant mountains; they strip away brambles and gather fragrant herbs, practicing the "bird-stretch" and "bear-stretch" exercises.
Yet, the golden furnaces rarely produce results, and the Jade Flowers are difficult to behold.
To speak of "congealed marrow transforming into bone" is merely empty talk;
to claim one rides upon rainbows or dragons is to have never seen their reality.
Some cast their bodies to the earth, while others lose their bones at Mount Tiantai.
In life, they lack the grace of nurturing;
in death, they receive no benefit from the unseen realm.
Their inverted minds are more precarious than those of common creatures.
The net of heterodoxy ensnares all living beings;
the nine clans prolong the calamity of destroying the orthodox,
while the six relations invite the karma of deceiving the sages.
To cling to the precarious and rely on the decayed is truly enough to chill one's heart; to remain haughty and unafraid—how extreme is such folly!
This is your sixth blindness.
An external treatise says:
Now, the phonetic systems of the Chinese and the barbarians differ;
yet, that which is called Śākyamuni in the Buddhist scriptures is a foreign (Hu) term.
When translated here [in China], it is rendered as "Capable Sage" (Néng Rú).
Because the title of "capable Confucian" is inferior to that of Zhou and Kong,
the inferior designation of "capable Confucian" is omitted,
and the non-Chinese (Rong) title of Śākyamuni is retained; that which is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* [is thus established].
In the language of Han,
"a-mu" means "no";
"anuttara" means "supreme."
Samyak-saṃbuddha means "perfectly and universally awakened";
it refers to the path of bodhi.
In this land, there already existed the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way (the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi), and the foreign Dharma was not considered different from them;
therefore, it was not translated.
Furthermore, as for the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
In the language of Han, this means "sentient beings with great wholesome minds.
This is designated as inferior and not as a superior person (*uttamapuruṣa*);
thus, its derogatory designation is concealed, and there is no corresponding translation for it.
Such are the examples of those classes that have not been translated;
they obscure the mundane world and delude the minds of beings.
Yet, to loathe the old and prize the new is a constant failing of the dissolute;
to detest what is common and favor what is different is likewise so.
Such is the vulgar sentiment of the common world that there are guests in Handan who crawl on their bellies [in submission],
and travelers from their youth who forget to return home.
The world cannot know this;
such is their seventh delusion. 7.
Regarding the "Untranslatable Index to the Inner Three Jewels," the seven internal admonitions state:
Now, names cannot grasp things;
they merely refer to actualities.
How could one use worldly, provisional discourse to determine the relative superiority or inferiority of the profound sages?
Now, the school of Xunzi names its chapters based on their substance,
while the Master Zhong (Mencius) fashioned his chapter titles based on mountains.
A mountain is higher than a mound.
Zhongren did not propagate the Master’s teachings;
his hair was merely gathered upon his ears.
As for Xunzi, his virtue did not equal that of Lao Dan.
How can the reputation of the Confucian scholar allow one to thus disparage the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius? Yet,
as for the title of Śākyamuni—
The meaning encompasses many aspects and can universally permeate all virtues;
it cannot be exhaustively defined by the single term "benevolence" alone.
Since benevolence is cut off from the four propositions,
how could one take what is capable of being determined and turn it back to describe it?
Having no other recourse, I must do so.
I have merely retained its former title.
Furthermore, it is said that the Daoist tradition has long possessed the term "Perfect Universal Knowledge" (Sambuddha).
As for the claim that "the Way and bodhi are not different," this is merely a case where followers of the later counterfeit teachings have falsely usurped this name.
If one were to examine the facts and trace the source, how could such a designation be justified?
Now, the supreme Dharma follows the lofty and victorious path, its principles pure and penetrating;
it rectifies the false and returns to the true by reversing the deceptive.
Thus, the talismans, incantations, and curses [of the Daoists] cannot be called correct.
When incense and rue are mixed together, one cannot call it true; thus, the talisman for warding off ghosts states:
"On the left, wear the Great Ultimate Talisman (Taiji Zhang);
on the right, carry the Kunwu iron [sword], pointing toward the sun."
He immediately halted his radiance and confronted the ghosts from a thousand li away; he fashioned the "Yellow Divine Transcendent Chapter" (*huangshen yuezhang*) for slaying ghosts.

He also created the "Red Chapter" (*chizhang*) method, which likewise kills people. He maintained the state of the female (*wei*), looking down upon the inferior while regarding it as the supreme; thus the Elder spoke.
"It is better not to act as the male, but to maintain the female. It also says:
"The nature of the Dao is close to water; one must clench the mouth and fix the eyes. How can this be called the Dao? Zhuangzi said:
To bandage the eyes of Li Zhu and clamp the mouths of Yang and Mo is like the warbling of spring birds;
it may resemble singing,
yet the birds lack the substance of being able to sing.
The "insect" (虫) that devours wood may approximate the character for "word" (字);
yet the "insect" lacks the true meaning of the character for "explanation" (解).
This is precisely what is meant by the confusion between name and reality.
Furthermore, the suspicion that "Bodhisattva" is not a transliteration is an error made even more severe;
the text states that the supreme sages penetrate even the most minute creatures.
All possess the designation "insect.
As the Sūtra says:
"Among those with many feet and two feet, the Tathāgata is most honored."
Yet, the state of hibernating insects extends to all sentient beings;
how could living beings transcend the categories of ordinary and sage?
The designation "great mind" does not apply to those who are inferior.
Though you may scour for flaws and seek out defects,
it cannot diminish the beauty of Nanwei; though you may clench your heart and mimic a wry smile,
[it cannot surpass the natural grace of the original].
The beauty of Xi Shi has not yet been altered;
I shall further explain its essential points for you as clearly as pointing at one's palm.
"Śākyamuni" is the manifest name of the Buddha.
Bodhi is the noble title for the Dharma;
the Bodhisattva is the leader of the Saṅgha;
these are the supreme designations for the Three Jewels.
The translator has preserved its original name;
it is not like the prophecy of the "Jade Pillar" at the Red Gate or the rhymes of the "Yang-father Yin-mother. As the *Huangshu* (Yellow Book) says:

Open the Gate of Destiny and embrace the infant True Man; turn the Dragon and Tiger and wear the Three, Five, Seven, and Nine. Unveil the celestial and terrestrial nets and open the Vermilion Gate; advance the Jade Pillar. Contemplate the Yin Mother as white as jade; contemplate the Yang Father. With hands rubbing and grasping, that which is called "horse dung" is the numinous newness.
To call spitting saliva "jade nectar" (yù yè) and clacking the teeth "celestial drum" (tiān gǔ);
to call swallowing saliva "sweet spring water" (lǐ quán) and horse dung "numinous firewood" (líng xīn),
while calling a rat "jade ore" (yù pó)— these matters from the *Shàngqīng jīng* (Scripture of the Highest Purity) are vulgar and unworthy of being displayed.
Their words are foul and difficult to manifest,
just as the numinous phoenix is rarely seen because of its dignified virtue,
while the mole rat hides its form out of fear because of its ugliness.
Although their physical forms are hidden, the fact remains that the ugly and the beautiful are distinct;
yet they remain in darkness, unaware of this—
this is the blindness of the seventh.
The external treatise says:
"Now, the Sage’s manifestations and transformations follow the regions to guide and lead beings;
among the Hu, he shaves his head and leaves his crown bare."
To reside in China, one wears the ceremonial cap and sash;
this is the constant form of distinction between the Chinese and the barbarians,
not a matter of victory or defeat in terms of religious teaching.
If the Buddha were merely to command the discarding of these crowns and black robes to don dark monastic garments,
thereby abandoning our refined customs to distance ourselves from the barbarian traditions of the Hu,
then he would be unable to fully comprehend the significance of the crown.
This would mean that his wisdom and power are not all-encompassing.
How can it be said that he manifests forms according to the various regions and establishes teachings accordingly?
If this were truly impossible, [then the claim would be false].
Thus, the Buddha would merely be a barbarian deity from India,
not a Great Sage of the Central Kingdom (Zhonghua).
How could the teachings of one with shorn hair be applied to a righteous state?
If one assumes a foreign form while practicing Chinese learning,
and merely shaving the hair is called "serving the Buddha," then by the same logic,
practicing Chinese customs while wearing a turban should also be considered "honoring the Way."
Thus we know that baring the head or binding the hair are different according to local customs.
Alas! If the common people employ these practices for the cultivation of goodness, one may truly say they value the tattered rags of their neighbors' homes.
To despise the ornamental patterns of one's own house while the world cannot recognize them—
this is the eighth delusion.
8. Uniform Regulation for Internal Divergent Directions. The eighth internal admonition states:
Now, the Ultimate Way responds to the times without fixed direction;
sages and worthies seize the opportune moment to lead all beings.
When the Master dwelt among the nine tribes of the Yi, he did not distress himself over their barbarism.
When Yu entered the land of the naked, he joyfully cast off his robes.
When the Duke of Zhou traveled to Yue, he tattooed his body.
King Wuling conformed to the ways of the world by adopting the clothing of the Hu;
although the methods of the trap and the snare differ,
the achievement of catching the fish and the rabbit is the same.
How much more so for those who transform their worldly ways and restrain their minds, alter their physical appearance and fix their resolve—
casting off hairpins and silken robes to gather with the Way,
and discarding beard and hair to cultivate the truth.
The sacred regulations are not in vain; they surely lead to results.
Yet benevolence and righteousness vary according to the three types of wandering, while even a thief like Zhi may rely upon the five virtues.
The holy teachings have endured for a long time, ultimately causing even a "rat-jade" to falsely assume its name. Liu Zi said:
"The people of Zhou called a dead rat 'jade-roughness' (yupó); the profound transformations of the Mystery are likewise subtle and hidden."
Consequently, the chicken and the phoenix were allowed to intermingle their forms, as Wenzi remarked:
"The people of Chu mistook the mountain chicken for a phoenix.
Thus, ninety-five species soared among the Western Rong tribes, while thirty-six sects became confused within the Eastern Kingdom.

As for the treatises of Ulūka, the scriptures of the master Vaiśeṣika, the Nirvāṇa [treatises]—which are the Vaiśeṣika doctrines—the Ṛṣi Agni-kaṇṭha (the non-Buddhist named Agni-kaṇṭha), the Ṛṣi Jala-kaṇṭha (the non-Buddhist named Jala-kaṇṭha), the path of Aṣṭaka Māṭhara, and the son of Ajita, the nihilist non-Buddhist: these either rely upon fire and water to seek the sages.
They rely on the sun and moon to emulate the divine;
they grasp at the four great elements as being without cause;
and they point to the three karmas as having no retribution.
Stagnant consciousness is as dark as the mountains of the netherworld;
the deviant mind is as murky as the valleys of obscurity.
Such are those of this ilk.
These are the heterodox doctrines of the Western lands.
Next come the ghostly laughter and spirit-talk, the peaceful songs and vast chants,
and the swallowing of swords and spitting of fire.
I am struck by the mediocre mind of Zhongqing,
who merely rinses in the rain and exhales the wind;
I am startled by the shallow deliberations of Liu An.
Some wear the registers of the Central Yellow upon their persons and recite the talismans of the Spirit-Fly;
they tread upon the Golden Gate and cause their spirits to roam.
Relying upon the Jade Capital to wash away karmic burdens—
such examples as these belong to the heterodox teachings of the Eastern Region.
All have their minds shrouded by the net of heterodoxy and their eyes pierced by inverted needles;
they dig deep moats of delusion and build high walls of doubt.
Each clings to a single corner of partiality, wandering lost within the three realms.
They contend to guard their two views, sinking into obscurity within the nine schools of thought;
they recognize the substance of saṃsāra,
yet ignorance obscures its abiding ground.
The mind’s functions are restless;
grasping at signs drowns its profound source.
The Great Sage, with his eye of the Path, foresaw this and administered medicine according to individual capacities.
Born in the Western Land, the True Teaching flowed to the East.
When illness was grave, he personally descended as the King of Physicians;
when affliction was slight, he entrusted remedies for distant transmission.
Subordinate generals were employed to eliminate the crows and mirrors;
eminent commanders were dispatched to slaughter the whales and sharks.
This, too, was the medical art of Jie and Bian within the Śākya school.
The Dharma King possesses the strategic power of Sun Wu and Wu;
the Sage has no dual systems of governance, for their outward forms and meanings are uniform.
It is like the clear Ji River and the turbid Yellow River, which both flow into the vast ocean and become of one taste.
Those with green throats and crimson foreheads gather upon Mount Sumeru, sharing its hue.
Zhonghezi said:
"Those who possess the patterns of the celestial sphere are all seeking the way of immortality as a transcendent."
Next, there is that which nourishes my physical life today;
by arresting its vitality and prolonging its splendor, perhaps it may reach three or five hundred years—
this is what I consider true.
The principle of longevity and far-reaching vision lies herein.
Yet, the methods studied by the Daoists of today no longer take this into account.
However, for the most part, [these teachings] merely aim to ensure that when the body dies, the spiritual intelligence (shenming) is reborn in a superior realm.
If one no longer values this body,
it would be better to devote oneself single-mindedly to studying the Buddha-way.
The Buddha-way cultivates the spirit so that it becomes clearer and more refined day by day;
it possesses profound principles and the methods of concentration and wisdom.
It can be practiced even by those who are frail; why labor under such arduous toil?
To call oneself a Daoist while in reality studying the monastic laws of the Buddhist school,
yet without specializing in either,
is surely the work of one who merely attempts to draw a dragon or paint a tiger.
"Why do you not discard your deer-skin cap and yellow-brown robes, shave your beard and hair, dye your garments saffron, and take refuge in the World-Honored One?

As for the scriptures and the principles of practice of the world’s Daoist practitioners, they are based on the *Sāṃkhya* and *Vaiśeṣika* systems; only after these are mastered do they speak of drawing upon the sūtras and śāstras of the Buddha’s school."
They rewrote Buddhist scriptures, such as the *Huangting*, *Yuan yang*, *Lingbao*, and *Shangqing* sutras, as well as the canons of the Three Sovereigns (*Sanhuang*).

They altered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha* sutras to create treatises on the cultivation of the mind. These practices relied upon seated meditation (*zuo chan*) while seeking spiritual responses; they changed the name of "seated meditation" to the term "contemplation of the spirit" (*si shen*). Among these, the *Shangqing* tradition was considered the most exalted.
Yet they have not transcended the realm of the higher heavens;
furthermore, the methods of the Transcendents of the Great Clarity (Taiqing) are likewise cast aside and left unmentioned.
It remains unknown what specific practices distinguish them from the Buddhist school such that they are called "Daoists."
Those who attain the Way should take the Buddha as their teacher.
You, sir, are a man of the South;
you have personally studied the methods of the Daoist Chonghezi of Mount Maoshan.
Chonghezi and Tao Yinyu constantly made it their practice to revere the Buddha-dharma;
whenever they encountered a group of monks, there were none whom they did not pay homage to.
Within the mountain caves, he installed Buddha images everywhere; leading his disciples and those students who came to study under him,
he practiced repentance morning and evening and constantly read Buddhist scriptures,
transcribing texts according to the *Xuánjī* (the astronomical sphere).
This was intended to restrain those who were not contemporary Daoists who did not revere the Buddha.
Thus, Tao Yinyu, in his letter to Dafa Master, said:
"I have gone beyond the calendar and heard the sounds [of the Dharma]."
This morning my eyes received these written words;
perhaps because of the merit accumulated through years of prostrations,
the True and the Responsive have thus manifested their presence.
Just now, having tidied my rush matting and gathered flower-water,
I have straightened my robes and composed my thoughts, awaiting the sound of your staff.
Your disciple, Tao Hongjing of Huayang, bows in homage.
"You have served as a disciple of the Buddha and revered the Sangha,
never before uttering a dissenting word.
Why do you now bring yourself to ruin by violating your own fundamental tenets?"
Unrighteousness and lack of benevolence invite the gravest punishments.
The *Lun* by Mouzi states:
"The transformations of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, and Laozi..."
To compare him to the Buddha is like comparing a white deer to a qilin;
that you cannot awaken to this is your eighth blindness.
The External Treatise says:
Prior to the nine cycles of the Heavenly Sovereign,
writing and seals had not yet been devised.
After the six hexagrams of Fuxi,
written characters emerged;
from that time onward, the recording of scriptures gradually flourished.
The former sages and ancient worthies all composed the classics;
the rites of yielding and ceding as well as the use of weapons are fully set forth in the inscribed records.
Thus, the Left Scribe and the Right Scribe recorded events and speech, respectively.

With upright brush and straightforward speech, free from affectation or falsehood, both the "Account of Foreign Nations" in the *Wei Shu* (Book of Wei) and the *Gao Shi Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Recluses) by Huangfu Mi state:
"The 'Sengmen Futu Jing' (The Sramana Buddha Scripture) was composed by Laozi. [This] refutation says: "As for the so-called 'Futu Jing,'..."
The *Weilüe* and the *Xiyu zhuan* state that the kingdom of Lin-yi has a divine personage named Śariputra, as recorded in the tradition.
Śāriputra was advanced in years and his hair had turned white;
he constantly taught people to follow the path of the Buddha.
Whenever anyone encountered calamity or misfortune, or those who were childless, [he would provide guidance].
He exhorted them to observe the Buddhist fasts and precepts, and to relinquish their wealth to atone for their transgressions. King Siṃhahanu had long been without a crown prince;
consequently, his consort Māyā performed a sacrifice to the Buddha.
A prince was born,
and his son was subsequently named Fútú (Buddha).
This occurred during the reign of Emperor Ai of the Former Han dynasty.
The King of the Yuezhi dispatched Qin Jing as an envoy, who orally transmitted [the teachings] to Jing.
Thus, the Buddhist scriptures and doctrines were already circulating sixty-three years after the early Han period.
Emperor Ming was precisely moved by this auspicious dream.
Examining Qin Jing’s biography of the transmission of the scriptures,
it does not state that Laozi preached them.

According to the records, during the Jin dynasty, the Daoist Wang Fu altered the *Xiyu zhuan* (Account of the Western Regions) to produce the *Mingwei huahu jing* (Sutra on the Manifestation of Power to Convert the Barbarians). In it,
he claimed that Laozi traveled to the Flowing Sands to instruct the barbarian kings in the teachings of the Buddha.
To claim that he transformed himself into a Buddha and that a Buddha had only then appeared is the height of slander and falsehood. Moreover,
Jibin is ten thousand *li* away from here.
They have already returned.
From the Qin and Han dynasties down to the present, merchants and envoys from the various states have arrived in succession without interruption;
yet none have reported that Laozi is there.
I have never heard it said that [the Sage] converted the Hu by preaching the *Futu jing* (Buddha Sūtra) or that he himself became a Buddha.

Preface to the Lecture by Prince Jingling of the Qi Dynasty (Shen Yue) (19) Preface to the Lecture and Verses by Shen Yue, Prince Jingling of the Qi Dynasty: How great indeed is the wondrousness of the Sublime Enlightenment! How marvelous it is! It is the ultimate of the marvelous. It transcends the reach of words and thought; it is the source of all dharmas. It is profound and subtle, vast and boundless. It is that which all Buddhas have realized and all sages have attained. It is the pivot of the universe and the foundation of all beings. It is the light that illuminates the darkness and the medicine that heals the afflictions. It is the supreme truth, the peerless path. To seek it is to transcend birth and death; to realize it is to enter Nirvana. How could one not revere it? How could one not cultivate it? May all beings together aspire to this wondrous state. May they all, through the power of this teaching, quickly attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus do I offer these verses in praise.
