Imperial Decree Explaining the Meaning of the Two Truths (II-1). Imperial Decree Explaining the Meaning of the Two Truths, along with Responses to Questions on the Principle of the Two Truths: The reality of these truths is indeed profound and mysterious.
Were it not for an empty mind,
there would be no way to communicate its vast profundity;
this is the method for clarifying the Way.
The reasons for this are not limited to one;
to state the essentials, they do not go beyond object and cognition.
At times, the meaning is elucidated by means of the object.
At times, practice is manifested through wisdom;
as for the two truths, this is clarifying the meaning by way of the object.
If one is confused regarding their direction, the three realms of existence will not cease.
If one reaches this ultimate point, all myriad entanglements are cast off.
As for what is called the Two Truths:
the first is the Truth of Ultimate Reality (paramārtha-satya).
The second is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
True truth is also called ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Conventional truth is also called worldly truth (*loka-satya*).
The *tattvasatya* (truth of reality) and *saṃvṛtisatya* (conventional truth) are established by name based on their definitive essence;
the *paramārthasatya* (ultimate truth) and *lokasatya* (worldly truth) are designated by way of praise and censure.
If one speaks according to their sequential order:
One should say: first, the ultimate truth;
second, the conventional truth;
and the synthesis of the one and the two.
As for their number, they are three;
it is not merely that their number exceeds two,
but they are also designated as having a sequence of before and after.
This is not convenient for the meaning.
Since the ultimate does not exist because of the conventional,
the conventional likewise does not arise from the ultimate.
It can rightly be said that there is one ultimate and one conventional.
"Ultimate" (zhen) means reality;
it is equality, wherein no other distinct phenomena exist.
It is capable of producing intermingling;
"the mundane" has the meaning of origination (*samudaya*),
for by this dharma, [birth] arises.
Superficiality and falsehood arise through conceptual construction.
"The ultimate truth" (paramārtha) is a distinguished name established in reference to the realm of non-arising.
It is said that this Dharma is most supreme and most wondrous, with nothing able to equal it.
"World" (loka) takes the meaning of separation;
it is characterized by arising and ceasing, flux, and movement, lacking any abiding mark.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"That which is known by those who have left the world is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
that which is known by those of the world is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)."
This is the textual evidence for the principle of praise and censure.
Although the two truths are established with different names and distinctions,
they are explained as having a single meaning through terms such as "the real" (satya), "the conventional" (saṃvṛti), and "the worldly" (loka).
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is explained by way of two meanings.
To speak correctly, since this principle is supreme in its qualities, it is also "ultimate" (*parama*).
Since the mundane is merely superficial and false, it possesses no further reality.
For this reason, it is given only the name "worldly" (*loka*).
As for "truth" (*satya*), its meaning is "thoroughly real.
True Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is that which is thoroughly real.
The conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is thoroughly real as conventionality;
the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is free from existence and free from non-existence,
whereas the conventional truth is both existence and non-existence.
To be both existent and non-existent is a provisional designation;
to be free from existence and free from non-existence is the Middle Way—
this is the true Middle Way.
It takes non-arising as its essence;
since the conventional is a mere provisional designation,
it takes arising phenomena as its essence.
29. (The Discourse on the Meaning of the Two Truths by Shi Hui-chao of Nanjian Temple) (21) Hui-chao of Nanjian Temple inquired, saying:
"That which arises through floating and falsity and is produced is called the conventional (saṃvṛti)."
That which is free from existence and non-existence is called "the True.
I do not yet understand whether this floating falsehood is of one essence with the True or whether it is distinct from it.
The Imperial Decree replied:
That which is known by worldly people has arising as its essence;
that which is known by those who have transcended the world has non-arising as its essence.
This treatise is composed based on these people.
It should be stated thus:
from the perspective of ultimate truth, that which exists is empty;
from the perspective of conventional truth, one points to emptiness as existence.
Based on this meaning, it is clarified that they cannot be distinct.
Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asks:
"If the ultimate and the conventional are said to be of one essence,"
I do not yet understand whether the Absolute Truth (paramārtha-satya) also possesses movement and activity.
Is it that movement and activity are self-generated and have no relation to the Absolute Truth?
Your Excellency’s reply further states:
The Truth is quiescent and devoid of any characteristic of movement;
it is only the deluded consciousness of ordinary beings that falsely perceives movement.
Again, he asked:
I do not yet understand whether it is because there is movement that ordinary people see erroneously,
or because there is no movement that ordinary people see erroneously.
The Imperial Decree further replied:
If there were movement, it would not be called a distorted vision.
It is because one perceives movement where there is no movement that it is considered a distorted vision.
Furthermore, he asked:
If dharmas have no arousal, then there should be only one truth.
The Imperial Decree further replied:
"This principle is eternally quiescent; this itself is the single truth."
To perceive movement as horizontal is yet another truth;
by this standard, there ought to be two [truths], and one cannot say there is only one.
Furthermore, I ask:
"Is there such a mistaken view, or is there no such mistaken view?
The Imperial Decree replied again:
"In speaking according to human perspective, such a mistaken view exists."
He further consulted:
"If one relies on human speech, there will be arbitrary views;
if one speaks based on the Dharma, one should not see any movement."
The Imperial Decree further replied:
"The Dharma is indeed motionless;
it does not obstruct those who perceive movement for themselves."

30. (The Prince of Jin’an, Xiao Gang, Consults on the Meaning of the Two Truths) (21) The Prince of Jin’an, Xiao Gang, Governor of Danyang, submitted this inquiry: [The text continues with the consultation.]
I understand that you distinguish between the "arising" and the "non-arising" based on the person who realizes the principle.
I have not yet determined whether this "floating emptiness" and "non-arising" are one and the same entity or if they are distinct.
The Imperial Decree replied:
"What ordinary minds perceive is its arising and movement;
what the sages perceive is its non-arising."
To argue based on benevolence (*ren*) as being of a different substance (*bhinnasvabhāva*) would mean that if they were identical in essence (*tādātmya*), they could not be different.
This has been explained in detail above and need not be discussed further.
Again he asked:
"If the true does not differ from the conventional,
and the conventional does not differ from the true,"
How can it be that what is seen by ordinary people has "arising" as its essence,
while what is seen by the sages has "non-arising" as its essence?
The Imperial Decree replies:
The conventional is immediately the realization of the ultimate; the ultimate is immediately the vision of the conventional.
Speaking from this perspective, they naturally constitute a non-duality.
Distinguishing views according to individuals, there is a difference between those that arise and those that do not.
Furthermore, I inquire:
I have not yet understood how the essence of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is both floating and illusory.
How can one perceive such floating illusions within the realm of ultimate reality?
The Imperial Decree replies:
The essence of ultimate reality is inherently devoid of floating illusions.
Those who are deluded construct arbitrary fabrications and claim that [reality] exists;
yet this does not harm the true reality, which is by its very nature void and profound.
Furthermore, he asked:
"The vision of the Noble Ones does not fluctuate,
whereas the vision of ordinary persons fluctuates."
Since flowing and not-flowing are distinct,
the ignorant claim they cannot be one.
The Imperial Decree replies:
It is not that the non-flowing and the flowing are each separate entities.
Rather, it is said that ordinary beings, within the state of non-flowing, erroneously perceive this flow.
Based on this, the argument can be established as a unity.
Again, he asked:
"The essence of true quiescence is fundamentally non-flowing;
yet ordinary beings perceive flow without ever departing from that true essence."
If that were so, there would be only one truth and the two truths could not be established.
In response to this instruction, it was said:
"The essence is eternally mutually identical; in principle, they cannot be different."

Generally, when ordinary people perceive the floating and empty, while sages behold the true and quiescent, based on this distinction between the ordinary and the sage, one may establish the names of the two truths.
(The Monk Huiyan of Zhaoti Temple Consults on the Meaning of the Two Truths) (21). Huiyan of Zhaoti Temple asked:
Ordinary beings perceive the conventional and take arising phenomena as their essence;
sages perceive the ultimate and take non-arising as their essence.
I do not yet understand the nature of arising and non-arising.
If one merely perceives their difference, on what basis can they be distinguished as one?
The Imperial Decree replies:
"Ordinary persons [perceive] the unconditioned within the conditioned."
The Sage thus distinguishes existence from non-existence;
yet existence and non-existence are mutually identical—this is what is meant by "the single essence.
Furthermore, [the interlocutor] inquires:
I have not yet understood what this "discourse on the One" refers to;
what is the name of this One?
Your Majesty’s decree replied:
Precisely because existence is not different from non-existence and non-existence is not different from existence,
it is called "one" and has no other name. Furthermore,
[the interlocutor] asked:
If non-existence is not different from existence,
and existence is not different from non-existence,
yet one perceives only one of them.
"What are these two?
The Imperial Decree replied:
'Ordinary people see them as existing; sages see them as non-existent.'"
Since these two perspectives have diverged, they form a duality.
Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asks:
"The Sage perceives non-existence; how can this be termed a 'Truth' (satya)?"
How can the perceptions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) be called truths?
The Imperial Decree replies:
"The perceptions of sages (*ārya*) are truths because they reside within the state of sagehood."
Ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) definitively claim that things exist; therefore, for ordinary beings, these are truths.
(32) (The Monk Yúnzōng of Qīxuán Monastery Consults on the Meaning of the Two Truths) (21) The Monk Tánzōng of Qīxuán Monastery asked:
"Does a sage perceive conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) or not perceive conventional truth?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"The sage knows that ordinary people perceive the existence of conventional truth."
If one discusses this, the Sage no longer perceives it.
Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asks:
"Since the Sage does not perceive conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),..."
Question: How does one teach and transform sentient beings by means of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)? Answer:
The Sage is free from delusion and thus does not perceive conventional truth for himself.
It does not hinder the Sage from knowing what ordinary beings perceive;
therefore, he conforms to the dispositions of sentient beings by teaching that there are two truths.
Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asks:
The Saint knows that ordinary people perceive conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Does this apply to the ordinary person as well?
The Master’s intent was to answer: "It does not."
This "ordinary person" is precisely conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Even the sage does not perceive this ordinary person.
Furthermore, he asked:
Since the Sage does not perceive the ordinary,
how can one know that the ordinary perceives conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)?
This is the response in the Imperial Decree.
Although the Sage himself is not ordinary,
he is also able to know that there are ordinary beings;
he regards them as existing.
Therefore, in order to accommodate their sentiments, he explained the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

(21) Wang Gui, the Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat, inquired regarding the essential meaning of the two truths (*satyadvaya*), saying: [The Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Wang Gui, inquired: "I ask:..."
I have not yet understood how, since the ultimate and the conventional are distinct,
they can possess the meaning of mutual identity.
Your Majesty’s decree provides the answer.
What the sage attains, he sees as non-existent;
what the ordinary person attains, he sees as existent.
Their perceptions of themselves differ.
There is no hindrance to the conventional not emerging outside of the ultimate.
Furthermore, I inquire:
I do not yet understand how it can be that there is no difference.
The term "substance" (zhì) carries two meanings:
does it mean that the meaning is distinct from the substance,
or does it mean that the meaning is identical to the substance?
The Imperial Decree replies:
We do not further distinguish between them, designating them as a single entity.
Yet, because the perspectives of the ignorant and the sages differ, they naturally constitute distinct interpretations.
Again, he inquired:
"Do ordinary persons see only the conventional, or can they also see the ultimate?
The Imperial Decree replied:
One can only perceive the conventional and cannot perceive the ultimate.
Again, he asked:
"Since their essences are mutually identical, why is it that one does not behold the ultimate?"
The Imperial Decree in response:
Generally, if one perceives the Real, one should not behold the mundane.
Since beholding the mundane is delusion, how can one perceive the Real?
34. (The Inquiry into the Meaning of the Two Truths by Śramaṇa Sengqian of Linggen Monastery) (21) Śramaṇa Sengqian of Linggen Monastery inquired:
"If the primary [truth] takes 'being without fault' as its meaning..."
"This is a name used for praise.
Being truly detached from the mundane should likewise be a name used for praise.
Emperor Wen replied:
This very essence is true;
it cannot be described by mere words of praise.
Since the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) has already been established with this elegant name, [it need not be further elaborated].
This is why he sighed. Furthermore, he consulted [the Buddha]:
"Since there is no one superior to me who has already received such praise and sighs of admiration..."
"My own substance is itself the Truth;
why, then, do you not praise it?
The Imperial Decree replied:
Because there is no one superior to me, I am worthy of praise;
yet my very essence is the Truth, and that Truth is also my true self.
Therefore, this is not mere flattery.
Furthermore, he asked:
"Since I am without fault,
why am I able to receive praise and acclaim?"
I am not false; how could this not be a praise?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"Not being false is the very name for the true reality."
To interpret the meaning according to human understanding is called "interpreting the meaning";
this merely accords with its actual substance—
how could it constitute praise?
He further consulted:
"This Dharma is such that none can transcend it;
how then can it be considered mere praise?"
The Imperial Decree replied:
"Since it is said that there is no emergence,
how could this not be a praise?"
35. (The Prince of Luoping, Xiao Zhengli, Consults on the Meaning of the Two Truths) (21) The Prince of Luoping, Xiao Zhengli, asked:
"I do not yet know whether conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is a produced phenomenon (*utpāda-dharma*) or not."
The Imperial Decree replied:
"The essence of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is precisely the nature of arising phenomena.
He further inquired:
Since worldly views are already arbitrary,
how could there be any arising?
This was the response given in the Imperial Decree.
To perceive perversely that things exist is why birth occurs.
Furthermore, he asked:
They are seen perversely as existent,
yet in reality they have no nature of their own.
Since they have no nature in reality, what can be said of their arising?
The Imperial Decree replies:
That which is called the "arising dharma" is precisely what is termed "transverse seeing," and that which is termed "transverse seeing" is precisely what is called the "arising dharma."
Again, he asked:
"If this is a mistaken perception, there should be no arising.
If there must be arising, how can it be called a mistaken perception?"
The Imperial Decree replies:
Since it is said that they are seen crosswise,
they are in truth themselves unborn.
It is merely perceived perversely as existing;
thus there is this perverse arising.
(36) (The Marquis of Hengshan, Xiao Gong, Inquires about the Meaning of the Two Truths) (21) The Marquis of Hengshan, Xiao Gong, inquired, saying:
I do not yet understand why, although the First Noble Truth (paramārtha-satya) already has a designation for its meaning, the Worldly Truth (saṃvṛti-satya) alone lacks a name for its meaning.
Let the Honored One provide an answer. The Master replied:
The world is already so superficial that there is no meaning to be discerned.
Furthermore, he asked:
"If there is no meaning to be discerned," [how can one speak of it?]
Why is it called "Truth" (satya)?
The Imperial Decree replied:
It is because ordinary people perceive it with certainty.
Therefore, the name "Truth" (satya) is established.
Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asked:
"If ordinary people perceive existence and thereby receive the name 'Truth'..."
Furthermore, ordinary people should also see that the characters for "attaining peace" (安義) have been obtained.
An imperial decree replied:
"Ordinary people clearly see [this]."
Therefore, the designation "Truth" (satya) can be established;
conventional usage is devoid of meaning.
How could one forcibly assign the name "meaning" to it?
He further consulted:
"Although worldly conventions lack ultimate reality,
they are not without their own conventional meaning."
Since such superficial customs already exist,
how could one not receive the title of "Master of Meaning" (Yiming)?
This was the response given in the Imperial Decree.
It is precisely because it is superficial that there is no meaning to be discerned.
If there were meaning to be discerned, how could it be called superficial?
(37) [The Monk Huizong of Zhongxing Temple on the Meaning of the Two Truths] (21) The monk Huizong of Zhongxing Temple said:
The Imperial Decree explains:
the Real does not depart from the mundane,
and the mundane does not depart from the Real.
I have not yet understood whether the ultimate truth is truly signless while the conventional is characterized by signs,
such that there is a distinction between signs and signlessness.
"How can they be of the same substance?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"The distinction between 'characteristics' and 'the absence of characteristics' lies in this very point."
Whatever exists as an object of perception is,
in fact, non-existent from the perspective of the noble ones;
this is the basis of our argument.
It may be understood that there is no distinction.
Again, he asked:
"Since it is a single dharma,"
"How can it be that seeing is divided into two?
Since seeing is already twofold, how could it be a single dharma?
The Imperial Decree replied:
Principle is indeed not dual;
it appears as dual only according to what is perceived by sentient beings.
Furthermore, he inquired:
"Since there are now two types of seeing,
do they not contradict one another?"
The Imperial Decree replies:
If dharmas were truly dual,
they could indeed be contradictory.
The Dharma is eternally non-dual;
it is people who perceive it as dual.
This treatise is composed on this basis.
How could they possibly be at odds?
Furthermore, [the interlocutor] inquired:
"People perceive that there are two."
One may speak of two people;
yet since the principle is one,
how could there be two?
The Imperial Decree in Reply:
"Although in principle there is no duality, it appears as two when considered in relation to persons.
(38) (Prince Xiao Ying, the fourth son of the Prince of Shixing, inquires regarding the meaning of the Two Truths. (21) Prince Xiao Ying, the fourth son of the Prince of Shixing, inquired, saying:
"The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is supreme in its meaning;
is it not also supreme in its virtue?
The Imperial Decree replied:
Since his realization of the meaning is supreme,
his virtue is likewise supreme.
Furthermore, he inquired:
"Direct speech is foremost;
it already encompasses both virtue and meaning.
Why then add the character 'yi' (meaning) to cause such prolixity?"
The Imperial Decree in reply states:
"Your direct statement that 'the foremost remains obscure in its meaning' is correct;
however, if one perceives the meaning of the foremost, it can be made entirely perfect."
Again he asked:
"If one adds the character 'yi' (義), it may achieve perfect beauty;
why not add the character 'de' (德) so that it may achieve perfect beauty?"
The Imperial Decree replied:
"The first is virtue;
how could it require further augmentation?"
However, by adding explanatory characters, both the virtue and the meaning become doubly excellent.
Furthermore, [the Master] consulted:
"To simply call it 'Number One' is sufficient to reveal its excellence."
The addition of honorific characters seems somewhat restrictive.
The Imperial Decree replies:
"First, it is to manifest virtue."
Furthermore, by adding explanatory characters,
both beauties are presented together;
how could there be any limitation?

39. (Prince Xiao Li of the Heir Apparent to the Prince of Wuping Consults on the Meaning of the Two Truths) (21) Prince Xiao Li of the Heir Apparent to the Prince of Wuping submitted this inquiry: [The text continues with the inquiry.]
The General Preface states:
"The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) are names established through praise and censure."
The two truths, the ultimate and the conventional, are established by name based on their definitive essence.
Since the principle of the ultimate truth is subtle and transcends both words and thought,
I do not yet understand how there can be the principle of a "definitive essence."
The Imperial Decree replied:
"To speak of its lack of characteristics and its being neither true nor untrue is to rely on provisional names and marks to explain the essence of true quiescence."
Again, he asked:
"If the ultimate truth has no essence,
how can its essence now be distinguished through provisional words?"
I do not yet understand why the truth of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*) is signless (*animitta*).
Why not employ words to discern its characteristics?
May Your Holiness deign to answer.
I offer these words to clarify the essence, yet I fear they may detract from its virtue.
If, moreover, I were to employ words to clarify its characteristics, it would burden that which is void and profound.
Furthermore, I inquire:
Ultimate truth is profound, void, and transcends verbal expression.
Since we now speak of "true existence," is this not merely relying on words to delineate its characteristics?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"It is by virtue of being entrusted with this name that it exists;
the name itself is a characteristic."
This does not contradict the principle that the signless is empty and quiescent.
Furthermore, I inquire:
I do not yet understand this use of provisional words to elucidate the essence.
"Is this in accordance with reason or not?
The Imperial Decree replied:

Furthermore, he asked:
"If one relies on words to explain names,
then the name will not correspond to the principle."
I do not yet understand what this correspondence intends to convey.
Your Imperial Decree replies:
"Although it does not accord with principle..."
In order to guide and lead sentient beings, one must employ names and signs in explanation.
(40) [The Inquiry on the Meaning of the Two Truths by Shi Huiling of Songxi Temple] (21). Huiling of Songxi Temple inquired, saying:
Ultimate truth has non-arising as its essence,
while conventional truth has arising phenomena as its essence;
yet it is said that non-arising is itself arising.
That which arises is itself non-arising.
Does this refer to the mutual identity within the substance,
or does it refer to the mutual identity within the meaning?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"In their essence, they are identical;
in their meaning, they are not identical."
Again, he asked:
"If the meaning is not identical,
how can the substance be identical?"
The Imperial Decree replied:
"Ordinary people perceive existence;
the Sage perceives non-existence."
From the perspective of conventional designation, they appear as distinct;
from the perspective of their essential substance, they are eternally identical.
Furthermore, he inquired:
Since the substance is not dual, why must there be identity?
The Imperial Decree replies:
"If the substance has no distinction, yet the two conditions perceive it as dual."
Since these two views differ, it is necessary to clarify that their essence is identical.
Furthermore, I inquire:
if this is how you understand the purport of the teaching, [is it so?]
The fruit is explained in terms of the person as being immediate;
this is the response to the Imperial Decree.
Based on the person's perspective, it is divided into two.
As for why the Two Truths are so named, to clarify this from the perspective of human perception would also present a great obstacle.
(41) [The Fifth Son of King Shixing, Xiao Ye, Inquires on the Essential Meaning of the Two Truths] (21). The Fifth Son of King Shixing, Xiao Ye, inquired, saying:
Zhen Di said, "It is called 'True.
Is it truly real?
The Imperial Decree replied:
Having attained this true reality,
he further inquired:
"When a Bodhisattva realizes suchness..."
"Does this mean one forgets both the mundane and the true?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"One forgets both the mundane and the true."
Therefore, it is said that one "converges with the truth.
Again, he asked:
"If one forgets both the conventional and the true, why is it said that one 'converges with the truth'?"
If one forgets both the conventional and the real, what can be called "truly real"?
In response to this decree:
if one preserves both the conventional and the real, what can be called "truly real"?
It is precisely because both are negated that it is called the "real truth.
Furthermore, he asked:
"If one forgets the conventional and forgets the true, yet this is the real truth, [then what of it?]"
One should also forget both the ultimate and the conventional; yet this is precisely the true conventional.
In response to the Imperial Decree:
it is by forgetting the conventional and forgetting the ultimate that one perceives the ultimate.
Forgetting both the true and the conventional, one manifests even more clearly that which is not conventional.
Furthermore, [the questioner] inquired:
"The Bodhisattva realizes the truth."
Since both the mundane and the real have been forgotten,
to now invoke "actual reality" would contradict reason.
This is the response to the Imperial Decree.
If one falsely calls the provisional "real," one will ultimately forget the true.
When both are forgotten, it is called the real.
What is meant by "contrary to principle"?
(The Inquiry into the Meaning of the Two Truths by Shi Faxuan of Xinghuang Temple. (21) Shi Faxuan of Xinghuang Temple inquired, saying:
The *Yizhi* states:
"Since conventional truth consists of both existence and non-existence, it takes the arising of phenomena as its essence.
However, it remains unclear how a phenomenon that possesses existence and an essence can be said to 'arise'."
If there is no "is" and no "dharma," how can there be the meaning of arising?
The Imperial Decree replied:
In conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), existence and non-existence are established in mutual dependence.
Since they are mutually dependent, both may be termed "arising.
Furthermore, he asked:
If both the two dharmas of existence and non-existence are equally termed "arising," then since the meaning of arising is one and the same,
there would be no difference between existence and non-existence.
The Imperial Decree replies:
Since both are what is perceived by ordinary beings, the meanings arising from them may equally be "existent" or "non-existent.
How could they not be different?
Furthermore, [the opponent] asks:
If there were a distinction between having and not having a result,
there should be both arising and non-arising.
The Imperial Decree replies:
Since they are established as names in mutual dependence,
they share the same meaning of "arising."
43. (The Marquis of Chengxiang, Xiao Zhi, Consults on the Meaning of the Two Truths) (21) The Marquis of Chengxiang, Xiao Zhi, asked:
"I have not yet understood the meaning of the designation 'First' [Truth]."
"Is this form dependent [on something else]?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"It is precisely a form that is dependent."
Again, he inquired:
"What is the nature of the primary signlessness (animitta) such that it stands in relation to anything else?
The Imperial Decree replied:
Since it is called "the foremost," how could it not be dependent?
Furthermore, I inquire:
The first is "relative" (prati).
Since it is called "first," it is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) that is relative to the first.
Why is it not called "the second"?
If the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is dependent and thus not termed "the second," then the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) should likewise be dependent and not termed "the first."
The Imperial Decree replied:
"If you refer to 'the first' as 'waiting,' that is already sufficient from the perspective of the meaning."
Without conventional designations,
the second [category] could not be established through mutual dependence.
Furthermore, he asked:
If the name "conventional truth" (saṃvṛti-satya) did not refer to a second [truth],
then the designation "first" would have nothing to rely upon for its definition.
This is the purport of the response.
First, regarding Praising Reality:
since it is said that they exist in mutual dependence,
worldly names are those things that depend [on others].
This can be understood directly.
(The Discussion on the Meaning of the Two Truths by Shi Fayun of Guangzhai Monastery) (21) Fayun of Guangzhai Monastery asked:
The realm known by the Noble Ones is the ultimate truth; however,
I have not yet examined the wisdom that is capable of knowing it.
"Is this the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
or is it the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)?
To this, the Imperial Decree replied:
That which is capable of knowing is wisdom;
that which is known is the object.
When wisdom comes into dark harmony with the object, it may be said that they are identical with the truth.
Furthermore, he consulted:
"Is it for the sake of a person of wisdom that this is the ultimate truth?"
This is conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
In response to the Imperial Decree:
if one calls a person who possesses wisdom "conventional truth," that is so.
Again, he asked:
"I do not yet understand how a person of conventional truth could possess the wisdom of ultimate truth."
The Imperial Decree in reply states:
"The Sage is able to forget the mundane;
it is for this reason that he possesses true wisdom."
Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asked:
"Since this person is fundamentally non-existent and unarisen,
they likewise should not be designated as a 'person'."
The Imperial Decree replies:
In the realm of non-arising, one cannot speak of a "person.
It is only by relying on names and appearances that one speaks of there being a person who is eternally present.
45. (The Inquiry into the Meaning of the Two Truths by Shi Huiling of Linggen Temple) (21) Huiling of Linggen Temple inquired, saying:
"Is it that one perceives existence within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)?"
Regarding the view that things exist within conventional truth,
the Imperial Decree replied:
"Within ultimate truth, one erroneously perceives the existence of the conventional."
Again, he inquired:
"Regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), is that which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) real or is it empty?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"This is an existence that is false and illusory.
He further inquired:
"Should one perceive it as illusory?"
Question: Is it that one perceives existence?
Answer: The Imperial Decree states:
One perceives it as falsely existent.
He asked again:
"In that which is without name or characteristic, how can one perceive that which possesses name and characteristic?
The Imperial Decree replied:
To perceive names and characteristics within that which is nameless and characteristic-less is why they falsely exist.
Furthermore, he asked:
Regarding that which is without name or characteristic, one falsely perceives it as existing;
it is like fire, which is hot,
yet a deluded person might say it is cold.
Can one find the characteristic of cold within heat?
If names and characteristics could exist where there are no characteristics,
then this cold should also exist within fire.
The Imperial Decree replied:
Fire is naturally hot; the perception of coldness is a false vision.
This is merely self-delusion; it is not a different [substance].
46. (Śramaṇa Huìxīng of Xiānggūng Monastery Inquires about the Meaning of the Two Truths) (21) Śramaṇa Huìxīng of Xiānggūng Monastery inquired, saying:
"As for the delusions of ordinary beings..."
"Is it that one is confused only regarding the ultimate truth,
or is one also confused regarding the conventional?
The Imperial Decree replied:
To perceive existence within true reality is delusion regarding the true;
since one perceives the conventional as existing, this does not constitute delusion regarding the conventional.
Furthermore, he asked:
"If one understands the conventional, one thereby attains understanding of the ultimate;
if one does not understand the ultimate, how could one possibly understand the conventional?"
The Imperial Decree replied:
"Ultimate truth is empty and still, yet the deluded mind does not comprehend it.
Although one does not comprehend the ultimate, what prevents one from comprehending the conventional?"
Furthermore, he asked:
"This mind does not understand the Truth;
regarding the Truth, it is indeed deluded."
If this mind has already understood the conventional,
it should not be deluded regarding the conventional. Regarding this,
the Imperial Decree replied:
To speak of them as real is a pervasive delusion;
to discern the conventional is to understand each within the manifold of the conventional.
(47) [The Inquiry into the Meaning of the Two Truths by Śramaṇa Sengmin of Zhuangyan Monastery] (21) Śramaṇa Sengmin of Zhuangyan Monastery inquired, saying:
Is the understanding of emptiness attained within the thirty moments of mind a true understanding,

"It may be called 'analogous understanding' (xiangsi jie).
He further inquired:
I do not yet know whether such resemblance constitutes the ultimate truth or the conventional truth.
Your Majesty’s decree replies:

Not seeing non-arising cannot be called true understanding.
Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asks:

Furthermore, the objects illuminated [by wisdom] should likewise be neither true nor conventional.
If they were neither true nor conventional, there would be three truths.
To this, the Imperial Decree replies:
Since the realm illuminated is itself non-arising,
and non-arising is the truth, how could there be three truths?

If the object is itself the true object,

(48) [The Inquiry on the Meaning of the Two Truths by Śramaṇa Fachong of Xuanwu Monastery] (21). Fachong of Xuanwu Monastery inquired, saying:
In ultimate truth, there is neither arising nor ceasing;

In principle, they are not distinct;
therefore, it is said that they are one.

Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asks:

"Is it not the case that what ordinary people perceive as empty and existent can be said to be one and the same?

(49) (The Monk Sengmin of Jianye Temple Consults on the Meaning of the Two Truths) (21) The Monk Sengmin of Jianye Temple asked:
The layperson asks: "When one speaks of 'understanding the mundane,' does this mean understanding the disparities of the mundane world?
Or does it mean seeing the mundane as illusory and false? May Your Holiness provide an answer.
The Imperial Decree replies:
It is simply because one observes that the conventional is inconsistent that one speaks of "understanding the conventional.
Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asks:
"The conventional truth is not merely inconsistent."
This too is false.
Why do you understand their inconsistencies yet fail to understand their falsity?
The Imperial Decree replies:
If one causes ordinary beings to understand the false,
this is actually to understand the true and not the false;
therefore, it is called "understanding the conventional."
50. (Shi Jingtuō of Guangzhai Monastery Consults on the Meaning of the Two Truths) (21) Jingtuō of Guangzhai Monastery consulted [the Master], saying:
"I have not yet fully understood how the Sage perceives the Truth."
"Is it seen gradually,
or is it seen all at once?
The Imperial Decree replied:
Gradually he came to see him.
He again consulted him,
his mind empty and free of signs.
Upon seeing this once, the myriad manifestations are simultaneously stilled.
I do not yet understand for what reason the vision of the Truth (tattva) must proceed by stages.
The Imperial Decree replied:
From the ordinary person to the sage,
although the depth of understanding varies, the truth itself is inherently empty and still;
this does not preclude the possibility of perceiving existence through gradual stages.
Again, I inquire:
I have not yet understood whether, upon attaining the signless once, all phenomena are simultaneously forgotten,
or if they are not entirely forgotten.
The Imperial Decree replied:
"Once one attains the signless (animitta), the myriad existents are entirely forgotten.
He further inquired:
If one attains the state of non-characteristic and forgets all phenomena,
one may likewise, by attaining a void mind, exhaustively realize that true realm;
it should not be perceived gradually.
The Imperial Decree in reply states:
"The Tathāgata’s assembly of quiescence is the ultimate realization of truth;
those of shallow practice and saintly status constantly perceive it only gradually."
Again, he asked:
"If one perceives that true reality can only be realized gradually and cannot be attained all at once,
then one should likewise forget all phenomena gradually and not be able to forget them all at once."
The Imperial Decree replies:
Because there are degrees of superiority and inferiority in understanding, there is gradual realization;
because one has forgotten the self and is without partiality, all phenomena are simultaneously quiescent.
51. Imperial Decree Explaining the Meaning of the Dharmakāya (21): Imperial Decree Explaining the Meaning of the Dharmakāya, Together with Questions and Answers.
The Dharmakāya is empty and quiescent, remaining far removed from the realms of existence and non-existence.
It stands alone, detached from cause and effect;
it cannot be known by wisdom,
nor can it be cognized by consciousness.
How could this be discussed through mere designations?
Yet, wishing to manifest the principle, one cannot remain silent;
therefore, one follows along with verbal expressions.
Thus it receives the designation "Dharmakāya.
In India it is called *dharmaśarīra*,
while in this land it is termed the "Dharmakāya."
If considered from the perspective of its actual substance, it is a designation for self-nature (*svabhāva*);
if considered from the perspective of verbal expression, it is a name established through mutual dependence.
"Dharma" has the sense of a norm or rule as its primary meaning.
"Body" (kāya) has the meaning of "substantiality.
Because it is the substance of the guiding rules (dharma), it is called the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
This brief explanation provides a rough description of its substance based on verbal discourse.
This is the eternally abiding body;
this is the vajra-body.
If one subjects it to further rigorous examination, however, it is not so.
If this concentration were truly adamantine, it would become a name and a mark;
if it were truly permanent and abiding,
it would then constitute a spatial location.
What is called "permanently abiding" is originally a provisional designation termed "vajra";
it is fundamentally a metaphorical explanation.
When discussing the substantial reality,
its nature is identical to that of non-arising;
therefore, it is said that the Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of dharmas.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The body of the Tathāgata is not a body;
this body is immeasurable, boundless, and leaves no footprint."
Without cognition and without form, it is ultimately pure.
This purity of non-cognition cannot be characterized as being "stainless," for it is called "wondrous existence" while simultaneously not being existence.
"Detachment and non-detachment constitute what is called the Dharmakāya.
(52) [Invitation from Tiqisi: Shi Huiyan Inquires about the Meaning of the Dharmakāya] (21) Huiyan of Tiqisi inquired, saying:
I do not yet understand how the Dharma-body, being without marks, could lack a substantial essence (tǐ).
How, then, can one employ the concept of "essence" to explain the meaning of "body"?
[The recipient] replies to the imperial decree:
Being nameless and signless, there is no substance to be discussed;
yet, by resorting to names and signs, the wondrous substance is not non-existent.
Furthermore, he inquired:
If one relies upon provisional names and marks, it is not that a wondrous essence does not exist;
thus, by relying upon provisional names and marks, they do not fail to constitute the signless.
This is the purport of the Imperial Decree.
Since it is said that names and characteristics are merely provisional designations,
this sufficiently clarifies that the ultimate reality is indeed without characteristics.
Furthermore, I inquire:
If one relies on names and marks [to describe it], in reality there are no marks.
Since in principle there are no marks, how could there be any substantial entity?
This was the response given in the *Lingzhi*.
I submit that if words are used to guide and regulate things, how could they themselves lack an essence?
Furthermore, I inquire:
words should likewise be used to guide and regulate things.
"It is not that it is no longer signless.
The Imperial Decree replied:
"From the perspective of the principle of regulating things and establishing norms, it is logically not the case that it is signless."
What is called "signlessness" fundamentally refers to the wondrous essence.
Furthermore, he inquired:
"Reality is originally signless."
One should properly use this to regulate all things;
how can one conceal this reality and forcibly produce verbal constructs?
The Imperial Decree in reply states:
"True reality is signless and is not something that can be glimpsed by those of recent study;
therefore, I have been accommodating those who are superficial."
It must be expressed through verbal signs.
(53) (The Discourse on the Meaning of the Dharma-body by Śramaṇa Fayun of Guangzhai Monastery) (21) Fayun of Guangzhai Monastery asked:
I do not yet understand whether the eternally abiding Dharmakāya is attained through the myriad practices.
The Imperial Decree replied:
It is that which is attained through the myriad practices within the path of names and marks.
Again, he asked:
"Since it is attained through the myriad practices,"
How can it be said that there is no mark?
If there were necessarily no mark, how could it be attained through the myriad practices?
This is the response from the Imperial Decree.
It is without name and without form.
How could there ever have been an attainment? It is only by relying upon names and forms that one uses provisional language to speak of "attainment.
Furthermore, he asked:
Since there truly are the myriad practices and one truly attains the fruit of Buddhahood,
how can you claim that because of signlessness there is absolutely nothing to be attained?
Thus, the Imperial Decree replied.
The questioner maintains that the myriad practices truly exist;
now it is said that the myriad practices are themselves empty.
How, then, could there be a real fruit to be attained?
Again, he asked:
"There are currently sentient beings who cultivate the myriad practices;
I do not yet understand why these are entirely said to be non-existent."
The Imperial Decree replies:
What is perceived by the common vulgar is called "existence.
Yet when examined through principle, the myriad practices are in reality non-existent.
Furthermore, he asked:
"The sutras state that what is eternally abiding is called 'wondrous existence' (miaoyou).
If it is merely a provisional designation, in what sense can it be called 'wondrous existence'?"
The Imperial Decree replies:
It is because one relies upon names and marks that "wondrous existence" is spoken of.
When principle transcends names and marks, what is wondrous and what is existent?
54. (The Inquiry into the Meaning of the Dharmakāya by Śramaṇa Sengmin of Zhuangyan Monastery) (21) Śramaṇa Sengmin of Zhuangyan Monastery inquired, saying:
"I do not yet understand how the dharmakāya is beyond all marks."
Wisdom cannot know it;
it is beyond all marks and beyond all cognition.
How could there still be the designation "body"?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"Being without name and without form, how could there ever be a body?
It is called the Dharma-body only because it is spoken of by means of provisional names and forms."
Again, he asked:
"It should also be said, by way of provisional designation and characteristics, that this is what is illumined by wisdom.
How can it be that it cannot be known by wisdom?"
It cannot be cognized by consciousness.
The Imperial Decree replied:
"It may also be designated as that which is seen by the eye of wisdom."
He asked again:
"If the wisdom-eye can see,
then it can also be known by wisdom."
"If wisdom cannot know,
then the eye of insight has nothing to see.
This was the response given by the Imperial Edict.
The eye of wisdom has no seeing,
nor is there any dharma that can be seen.
Again, he asked:
If it is said that there is no seeing, what Dharma-body could there be?
The Imperial Decree replies:
"The principle transcends hearing and seeing; in reality, there is no Dharma-body."
Again he asked:
"If there were no Dharma-body, there would be no perfect enlightenment.
Since perfect enlightenment exists,"
"Is it not the case that the Dharma-body exists?
In response to this imperial decree, [the Master] replied:
"Because it is always expressed through provisional words, there is 'Perfect Enlightenment' (Sambodhi)."
Since the Perfectly Awakened One has already spoken by way of metaphor, how can the Dharma-body be definitively said to exist?
(55) [The Inquiry into the Meaning of the Dharma-body by Shi Fachong of Xuanwu Temple] (21). Fachong of Xuanwu Temple inquired, saying:
I do not yet understand whether the title "Dharmakāya" refers specifically to the wondrous primordial source,
or if the sixteen-foot golden form is also the Dharmakāya.
The Imperial Decree replied:
If discussed from a general perspective, both the provisional and the ultimate are so;
if discussed from a specific perspective, it refers only to the eternally abiding.
Furthermore, he asked:
If it were restricted to being eternally abiding, it should not possess a physical body.
If it is taken to include the sixteen-foot form,
how can that sixteen-foot form be called the Dharma-body?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"Since the eternally abiding [Dharma] already possesses a wondrous essence,
how could it be without a body?"
Even the sixteen-foot [form] can serve as a model for all things;
therefore, it may be universally designated as the Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, I inquire:
If one is eternally abiding and free from all attachments, only then can one be called the Dharmakāya.
How can the six-foot form, which possesses attachments, be called the Dharmakāya?
The Imperial Decree replied:
Sentient beings gaze up with longing and falsely perceive [the Buddha] as being sixteen feet tall.
Since these sixteen feet do not truly exist, what actual burden could there be?
Furthermore, he asked:
If the sixteen-foot [form] does not exist, what would one point to as the body?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"It is said that there is a response-body (nirmāṇakāya) because it appears according to the perceptions of sentient beings."
Again, he asked:
"Since you speak of the 'response body' (nirmāṇakāya), what is meant by the 'dharma body' (dharmakāya)?
The Imperial Decree replied:
Because it distinguishes based on general characteristics, it encompasses both the fundamental and the manifested;
yet when investigating the ultimate reality, it does not reside in the golden form.
(The Inquiry into the Meaning of the Dharmakāya by Shi Huiling of Linggen Monastery) (21). Huiling of Linggen Monastery inquired, saying:
I do not yet know whether it is because of "ultimate wisdom" that it is called the Dharma-body,
or because of the "transcendence of marks" that it is called the Dharma-body.
The Imperial Decree replied:
That which is nameless and signless is the Dharmakāya as the treasury of accumulation;
perfect and ultimate wisdom is the Dharmakāya of true gnosis.
Furthermore, he asked:
If there is no name and no mark, then there is neither body nor non-body.
Since there is already the Dharma-body, how can it be said to be without marks?
The Imperial Decree replies:
It is precisely because it is signless that it is called the Dharma-body.
Again, he asked:
"If it is because it is signless that it is called the Dharma-body..."
[The opponent asks: "In that case, wisdom and its names and marks would no longer be the Dharma-body.
[The Master] replies:
"Since it is wisdom without marks, how could it not be the Dharma-body?"
Again, he asked:
"If there is a body, how can it be called formless?
If it is formless, how can there be a body?"
The Imperial Decree replied:
"The Dharma-body is provisionally taught through names and marks that do not exist.
Furthermore, [the Emperor] inquired:
If the Dharma-body is provisionally said to reside within names and forms,
how can one point directly to the signless and call it the Dharma-body?
Let Master Lingzhi answer.
Since names and characteristics are provisionally established within the signless, how could one speak of the Dharma-body as being distinct from this signlessness?
(21) Shi Jing’an of Lingwei Monastery inquires on the meaning of the Dharma-body: Shi Jing’an of Lingwei Monastery asked:
I do not yet know whether the Dharmakāya manifests through responsive transformations or not.
The imperial decree replied:
"The Dharmakāya has no responsive transformations."
Again, he asked:
"Originally, it was because of responsive transformation that you spoke of the Dharma-body.
If there were no responsive transformation, what would be called the Dharma-body?"
The Imperial Decree replies:
"The Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is defined by its essence as the fundamental principle of the norm.
Discourse concerning the manifested transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) is not what we maintain here."
Again, he asked:
"If there were no manifested transformation (nirmāṇa), how could one serve as a model?
Since you have become a model for sentient beings, how could it be that there is no manifested transformation?"
The Imperial Decree replies:
Because sentient beings look up to him with devotion and receive benefit,
it is said that he "can serve as a model."
"Once the work of transformation is finished, what remains to be transformed?
He further consulted:
"If one can benefit sentient beings, that itself constitutes the fulfillment of transformation."
If there were no responsive transformations (nirmāṇakāya), how could one benefit sentient beings?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"By being able to inspire devotion and reverence, the model for practice will naturally be established."
Why trouble the Perfected One to stoop to respond to the mundane world?
Furthermore, we inquire:
since they have already given rise to such profound veneration, could it not be that there is a manifestation of their transformative power?
If there were no one to respond through transformation, what benefit would there be for those who look up with devotion?
The Imperial Decree replied:
"It is precisely because the World-Honored One is supremely divine and wondrous, and exceptionally profound."
It is simply by causing one to look up with devotion that one naturally receives blessings.
If benefits were granted only after a response had been made,
how could it be called the Ultimate Spirit?
Since it increases [the merit] even when not appropriate,
it achieves the ultimate excellence of beauty.
If one insists that it must be real, how would it differ from that of a Bodhisattva?

63. Letter to Marquis Guangxin (21). [Letter] to Marquis Guangxin. Prince Wang of Jin’an bows his head.
It has been some time since we last heard from you, and I have often felt a sense of longing and delay.

I humbly learn that you have personally attended the Dharma assembly of Vimalakīrti, where you received the golden words from his own lips.
Your eloquence is as precious as that of the Deer Park, and your principles accord with those of Vulture Peak.
The subtle and secret treasury having thus flourished here,
the adornment of the *bodhimaṇḍa* has from this point onward been further expounded.
How could it merely be that the lamp of the mind shines brightly through the night?
It is as if the filaments of the mind have already flown forth at dawn;

Now, one accompanies the chariot of the ten wholesome deeds.
Opening the path of the eight rectitudes,

Thus, these spring blossoms shall become autumnal fruit.
Whenever Your Majesty recalls the sublime assembly at Huālín, I too have been granted a place among the lowly ranks,

Hand in hand we ascended the heights, engaging in conversation and laughter;

Now, this volume considers only a single corner of the transmission of the vehicle.
The rain of the wisdom of hearing flows down in torrents, filling me with boundless joy;

Conditioned by ignorance, there is craving; lamenting one's own difficulty in being uprooted from it,

Feeling ashamed, I recite with my mouth yet lack the discernment of my mind;

Sentient Beings Know Meaning (by Shen Yue) (22). The Buddha’s knowledge is not different from the meaning known by sentient beings.
By Shen Xiuwen: "Buddha" means awakening (*buddha*).
Awakening means knowing.
From the stage of an ordinary person to the ground of Buddhahood,
the establishment of what is good and what is evil has never been different. However,
that which is known at the ground of Buddhahood is the correct path for attaining what is good.
That which is known by ordinary persons is the deviant path that loses what is wholesome.
The knowledge of ordinary persons regarding the attainment of the right path is no different from the knowledge of the Buddha;
it is simply because they take what is wholesome to be non-wholesome that they lose the right path.
Thus, one should know that the knowledge of ordinary beings and the knowledge of the Buddha are not different.
This is because while the objects of knowledge differ, the knowledge itself does not;
it is not that what is known by ordinary beings is not called "the object of knowledge" (jñeya).
While one may be seeking what is good, one may nevertheless arrive at what is not good;
yet if one accumulates this mind that seeks the good,
one will eventually find the path leading back to goodness.
Or, upon finding the path, one reaches the Buddha.
This is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings;
it truly resides in the constant transmission of their knowing nature.

66. The Meaning of Successive Rebirth in the Six Realms Leading to Buddhahood (Shen Yue) (22). The Meaning of Successive Rebirth in the Six Realms Leading to Buddhahood by Shen Yue: The Wisdom of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the sentient beings of the five paths and six realms.
There is a shared capacity for cognition;
there is no differentiation between them. Question:
"Is sensation knowing or non-knowing?
He replied,
"Neither."
Question: What constitutes its essence?
Answer: It is the non-extinction of the continuum.
Because the continuity is not extinguished, it is able to receive and know.
If the merit of cultivation and refinement accumulates gradually in this life,
then the principle recognized by the consciousness in future results will become increasingly refined.
The refined awareness is transformed so that it responds [to conditions] until reaching Buddhahood, remaining uninterrupted and unceasing.
If one produces ignorance in this life, then the consciousness of future fruits will become increasingly obscured.
The cognition that transforms darkness likewise comes forth to respond, reaching even unto the six realms of existence.
The instruments of receiving cognition receive and know according to conditions.
The beauty or ugliness of what is known does not pertain to this faculty that receives knowledge.
A questioner asked:
"I have already understood your instruction that knowing is not itself the knower."
The cognition of sensation is itself a continuity that is not extinguished;
this cognition arises naturally from within causes and conditions.
It is related to the instruments of this cognitive sensation through the principle of *li* (principle).
The answer is:
There is this continuity that does not perish, which arises naturally from within cause and effect;
there is cause and there is effect.

The Meaning of Causes and Conditions (by Shen Yue) (22). Regarding the meaning of causes and conditions, Shen Yue states: The nature of all sentient beings...
There is none who does not delight in life;
yet the paths sought for survival are uneven and manifold.
Thus, as beings drift through transmigration, their routes and destinations differ from one another.
In the space of a single thought-moment, manifold conditions arise in mutual interplay;
yet within the relationship of one cause and one effect, there may be discrepancies.
The nature that favors life is the same across all ten thousand species.
That which is naturally received is not established through conditions;
thus we know for certain that the arising of pleasure is not caused by conditions,
and that conditions are not pleasure.
Although birth involves dwelling together within the same physical form, each is nonetheless a distinct entity.
Once a single thought-moment summons a multitude of conditions,

Alas, how lamentable! Eulogy for the Dharma Master Kumārajīva (Sengzhao) (23) By Shi Sengzhao: Now, the Way does not manifest itself; it is propagated by those who embody it. It is only through the person that the Way flourishes. If the Way were to flourish without a person, then even the sages of antiquity would have had no need to appear. But since the Way must rely on a person to spread, it is the person who is the primary vessel of the Way. Therefore, when the Way is about to flourish, a worthy person appears; when the Way is about to decline, a worthy person perishes. This is why the Way and the person are said to be mutually dependent. The Dharma Master Kumārajīva was a man of profound wisdom and vast learning. He was born in the kingdom of Kucha in the Western Regions. From his youth, he possessed a keen intellect and a sharp mind. He was naturally inclined toward the Mahāyāna and deeply understood its subtle principles. His mastery of the scriptures was such that he could grasp their essence with a single reading. His eloquence was so fluent that he could expound upon them without end. He traveled extensively throughout the various kingdoms of the West, seeking out and collecting rare texts. He brought back over three hundred volumes of Mahāyāna sutras and śāstras, which he translated in Chang’an during the reign of Emperor Yao Xing of the Later Qin. His translations were elegant and precise, capturing both the spirit and the letter of the original works. His contributions to the propagation of the Buddha’s teachings in the East have been immeasurable. Now, he has passed away. Alas, how lamentable! The Way has lost its vessel; the teachings have lost their guide. How can we not mourn? I, Sengzhao, being one who once received his grace, now compose this eulogy to commemorate his virtues and to ensure that his legacy remains known to future generations. May his spirit rest in peace. A Biographical Account of Dharma Master Jing of Mount Lu’s Incense Burner Peak Temple (Yú Xī) [2–3] The Dharma Master’s name was Sēngjǐng. He resided at the Incense Burner Peak Temple on Mount Lu. His secular surname was Yú. His ancestors were from Wèiyáng in the commandery of Jīn. During the Jiànhé era of the Jin dynasty, they moved to the capital. His grandfather, Yǔ, served as the Governor of Lù. His father, Xiāng, served as the Magistrate of Zhōngshān. Both were men of great virtue and integrity who enjoyed the esteem of their contemporaries. Master Jing was born in the second year of the Yǒngchu era of the Qi dynasty. From childhood, he possessed a spirit of detachment; he took no pleasure in worldly affairs and found joy only in the Way. At the age of seven, he entered the monastic order under the tutelage of the Venerable Sēngyuán of the Zhìyǎn Temple in the capital. He received the full precepts at the age of twenty. His conduct was pure and his discipline was strict. He was diligent in his studies and profoundly understood the subtle meanings of the scriptures. He traveled extensively to visit various masters, seeking out those who excelled in specific doctrines to resolve his doubts. His fame spread throughout the realm, and he was honored by both the high and the low. In the third year of the Tiānpíng era, he retired to Mount Lu. There, he lived in seclusion among the peaks and valleys, devoting himself entirely to meditation and cultivation. He maintained a simple lifestyle, relying solely on the offerings of the faithful. His character was serene and dignified, and his influence extended far and wide. In the first year of the Tàihóng era of the Liáng dynasty, he passed away at the temple on the peak at the age of sixty-seven. He was buried according to the rites on the mountain. I have thus set forth this account with evidentiary detail, hoping that his fragrant legacy will endure without reproach. Discourse on Monastic Midday Meals (Shen Yue) (24). Discourse on Monastic Midday Meals by Shen Xiuwen of the Southern Qi. Regarding why persons are unable to attain the Way:
The mind and spirit become clouded and deluded because they are disturbed by external objects.
It is due to these external objects that the mind and spirit are thus clouded and deluded.
The greatest disturbances are threefold:
first, power, profit, and illustrious fame;
second, the seductive charms of the beautiful and the voluptuous.
Third, there are sweet delicacies and rich, fatty foods;
though honors and fame occupy the mind daily,
they do not impose a burden for even a moment.
The allure of the seductive and the voluptuous is already profound;
the indulgence in sweet delicacies and rich flavors is an even more immediate burden.
Thus it is with the myriad affairs of the world.
These are all merely branches and leaves of these three things.
The Sage knew that if one did not sever these three matters, there would be no way to attain the Way through seeking it;
thus, he could not help but establish laws for them so that they would be simple and easy to follow.
If one were to simply say that these three matters are the root of delusion and should all be strictly prohibited,
one must recognize that these three matters are precisely what human sentiments are most prone to delude themselves over.
Thoughts and anxieties are difficult to dispel;
although there is the intent to prohibit them,
it is difficult for matters to be immediately followed accordingly.
It is like using a double-hulled boat to cross a river;
who would not wish to reach the opposite shore directly?
Yet the current of the river is already swift.
There is no principle by which one can reach the goal directly;
one must inevitably follow the current of heterodox and debauched ways for a long time before finally arriving.
It is not that one does not wish for haste, but rather that the matter is difficult to accomplish.
There must be a specific rationale for prohibiting these three matters.
Why is this? For humans, food cannot be discontinued abruptly;
yet, in terms of one's nature and disposition, nothing is more detrimental than these three burdens.
Therefore, by shifting this late meal to the midday and morning periods,
one remains pure, vacant, and free from affairs from after midday onward.
Because of this lack of affairs, one's thoughts and concerns become simplified.
At the beginning, one is not yet focused;
after a long time, one becomes habituated through practice.
Thereupon, one is bound by the eight branches.
Bound by prohibitions and precepts,
the desires for the beautiful and the alluring have no way to approach;
fame and worldly burdens are gradually dispelled as they arise.
Therefore it is said that the Buddhas of antiquity did not eat after midday.
This is surely a "trap" (quanti) for casting off burdens and a "shortcut" (jiejing) for attaining the Way.
Yet some maintain that it consists merely in abstaining from food;

His mind was expansive and clear, free from conflict with any being;
those with whom he shared close friendships were all the eminent men of the age.

As he spoke these words, Zeng shed tears, cast down his brush, and was overcome with grief.
Liu Zhilin bows his head repeatedly.
