Thus, among all classes of sentient beings and the multitudes of living creatures,
there are none who do not dedicate their persons to offer loyalty.
Those who do not serve as ministers to the King will fail to exert their utmost strength to honor and practice filial piety;
those who do not respect their own parents will likewise fail to do so.
Although the three chapters of the law may be relaxed and the three-foot code may be lightened,
if even one of these [transgressions] exists,
the three thousand [rules] become grave.
Yet they were not subjected to severe punishment nor placed under heavy censure;
was this not because the systems of Daoism and Buddhism differ in their regulations from those of Yao and Confucius?
To inflict injury and destruction is utterly contrary to ritual propriety;
the lotus flower is not the hue of a tied sash,
and the palm leaf differs from the principle of chiseled jade tablets.
People take the girdle as their standard insignia;
in the Way, one wears a cap but does not wear a girdle.
People take the binding of the hair as an ornamental adornment.
To explain: to fall away and find no place of acceptance is not to be disloyal to one's state;
to leave one's home is not to be unfilial to one's family.
They emerge from the dregs of the mundane world, severing their affection for sovereign and parent;
they wrest themselves from sensual desires, casting aside worldly sentiments toward wife and child.
Thus, the principle is fundamentally distinguished according to the categories of things.
It cannot be fathomed or examined by ordinary standards.
Among those to whom one owes life, none are more important than one's parents;
yet as a child, one does not offer thanks to them.
No gift is more profound than that of Heaven and Earth,
yet things do not respond to it;
the grace of a sovereign and a parent transcends the realm of names and forms.
Could it be that prostrating oneself with one’s head to the ground can repay even a ten-thousandth part of this?
Regarding those who have left the household life,
how could it be said that they owe no repayment whatsoever to their sovereign or their parents?
In every thought-moment, one must take the aspiration for the human king as the foremost vow;
through the Four Noble Truths, one brings great benefit to one's parents,
thereby dispelling the dust of kalpas and forever departing from birth and death.
How could it be limited merely to kneeling as the height of loyalty or providing physical care as the essence of filial piety?
It must surely encompass the mundane realm.
If one were to place him in a Confucian academy,
making him humble his appearance and lower his etiquette,
then there would be no filial impiety greater than the failure to continue one’s lineage.
Why not regulate them through marriage?
There is no greater lack of loyalty than failing to serve as a subject;
why not require them to call themselves "ministers" (chen) and "concubines" (qie)?

To take the kāṣāya as court attire and to prostrate while addressing oneself as "the poor practitioner" (pindao) results in a dual failure of ritual decorum and a simultaneous contradiction of one's title.
I deeply fear that the benefit of a single knee-bend does not exceed the dignity of the Ten-Thousand-Chariot Sovereign,
and that the toil of a single prostration merely serves to manifest the decline of the three robes.
If these things are deemed unacceptable, how could they be right?
A true king has no father, yet he serves the Three Elders as a father;
he has no elder brother, yet he serves the Five Venerables as an elder brother.
The honor accorded to a ruler also has its objects of reverence;
it is the respect shown to the ritual robes, not necessarily to the person themselves.
If one were to diminish their number, one would thereby debase the Way.
If one merely counts [the faults] while deprecating the Way, then the Way itself will be deemed deficient.
How can this compare to maintaining reverence within oneself and preserving the Way toward all things?
When reverence is maintained, one finds fulfillment;
when the Way is present, all things are honored.
One honors the Way precisely because one reveres all things.
To revere external things is also a means of honoring oneself;
how much more so since the physical form is like one's own body and the Way is like its shadow.
The body is like sound,
and the Way is like an echo;
when the form moves, the shadow follows.
When a sound is raised, its echo responds;
when the Way is honored, its form receives favor.
When the person declines, the Way ceases.
How could the Way by which one dwells be made to submit to a body that exists outside the Way?
How could a person who transcends the mundane world be made to maintain the reverence found within the body?
Furthermore, those who preserve the One and dwell in the Way do not depart from the secular world.
If that which is worthy of prostration were called the Way of the secular, and if the secular could participate in the Way,
then there would be two [ways] where there should be one, and the Way would not be practiced with singular focus.
How, then, can one maintain the ultimate sincerity of single-mindedness while demarcating the constant boundaries between the secular and the Way?
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*,
one should revere the kāṣāya as one would revere a Buddha stūpa;
that is to say, the kāṣāya is regarded as a "field of merit" garment (*puṇyakṣetra-cīvara*).
The robe is named "Emaciation," because it can emaciate afflictions;
the armor is named "Patience."
It is that which can subdue the armies of Māra;
it is also a metaphor for the lotus flower being unstained by mud;
and it is the banner-sign of all Buddhas.
Thus, the significance of the *kāṣāya* is supreme.
Were one to damage these Buddha-stūpas or destroy those victory banners,
one would be slighting forbearance and further degrading the field of merit.
I am filled with grave uncertainty and remain utterly confused regarding what to adopt and what to reject.
To cast off my robes and prostrate would violate secular custom and fail the ritual requirements of the ceremonial cap;
yet to adjust my formal attire and approach with hurried steps would render the black-clad monk’s garb inconsistent with the protocols for paying homage to the sovereign.
Therefore, he practiced meditation in the secluded precincts of Śrāvastī and withdrew from the high gates of the nobility;
his principles were severed from court audiences, and his affairs diverged from the pursuit of honor and audience with the sovereign.
Is it not said that I honor his Way?
That is why he requested his coming.
Having invited him, to treat him with such lowliness—what purpose would that serve?
Mount Lu is a dwelling place for those of virtue and the Way;
it is not subject to the process of selection and culling.
The *Gantang* tree was where the Magistrate rested while hearing lawsuits.
Thus, one should cultivate thoughts of not cutting them down;
for mountains and trees are without intentionality,
yet they preserve all things through their virtue.
The abundance of the Dharma and the Way—
how could one exalt the Way while neglecting humanity?
As the saying goes:
If a person can broaden the Way, then the Way must also be practiced by that person.
Although the rank of the Wangren (the King’s attendant) is humble,
he stands above the feudal lords.
How could those who practice the Way further disparage their rituals?
If it is claimed that both [parties] are practicing deception,
then one may simply abolish them both.
The way to suppress them is what is called "clearing away by mowing and weeding.
In this, that which is seized is vast;
how could it be limited to mere subjugation and humiliation?
If one claims that the two serve as a supportive aid,
then they ought to be honored;
the way to honor them is precisely what is meant by treating them with reverence and esteem.
How can one revere and honor the Way by causing it to be treated with reverence?
Even if one uses gold and jade to fashion a true image,
it is not through the gold and jade that solemnity is increased.
One honors the straw dog as a sacred image, yet does not treat it with contempt because it is made of straw.
Solemn reverence is ultimately entrusted to the Way; its weightiness or insignificance does not depend on the physical object.
That things cannot displace the Way is just as the Way constantly follows along with things;
yet the śramaṇa has arbitrarily imposed [this distinction] upon himself.
It is the reliance upon the dharma-robes that constitutes nobility;
there is none who does not revere these dharma-robes—how could it depend on the person?
The principle of not prostrating is a doctrine of lofty significance, rooted in the sūtras and vinaya.
The entrustment of the Dharma to kings is for the purpose of providing support and protection;
the Dharma is eternal.
Being eternal, its practice is unchanging.
If a single corner is rectified while a thousand gates may still falter,
there will be resources for the protection of the Dharma when it is open,
yet the danger of its collapse remains when it is closed.
Rather than letting it fall, why not protect it?
Why must one constrain oneself within the appearance of a monk or perform ritual circumambulations in dharma robes?
How could those who cause the myriad nations to take refuge find even a mere speck of obstruction between themselves and their goal?
As the saying goes, "Benefit others by means of what they themselves find beneficial.
Thus, the art of benefiting others may also be achieved by following the depth of their own refined understanding to bring them benefit.
When the sunlight shone above and the imperial destiny was established as the sovereign,
the ocean joined the celestial river and the branches were linked to the precious edifice;
thus, one relies upon the Unsurpassed Way.
He expounded upon boundless achievements;
though his lineage differs from other clans, respect for him remains as lofty as for those of antiquity.
His divine foundation and spiritual lineage—how could the Way be restricted by the present?
This is the first of the most grievous matters.
The precious mandate of the Eastern Kingdom of Yuezhi depends upon this;
the profound waves of the water of concentration and the colorful moisture of the clouds of Dharma provide its nourishment.
It celebrates the joy of sublime liberation and unfolds the blessings of eternal abiding;
even the former emperors of yore still observed this.
The sovereign is sagely and the ministers are virtuous; why, then, has this transformation occurred?
Your servant is so dull-witted that though he has considered the matter a thousand times, he has not once found a solution.
If, perchance, these innovations prove of no benefit to the future, [it would be a great loss].
If one incurs even a hair’s breadth of transgression over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
then even if the entire realm were to crush their heads and all living beings were to grind their bones to dust,
how could this possibly suffice to atone for the responsibility of such hidden faults?
To remit the crime of disloyalty—
this is the second most unacceptable course of action.
This is why I am so earnest in this matter and so sincere in my devotion.
Scratching my head and feeling my heart, I lay bare my liver and gall.
I prostrate myself and pray that Your Sacred Court will restore the Supreme Teaching,
so that the Nanda Garden may flourish forever and the Wheel of Dharma turn eternally.
If one wholeheartedly records such a person,
their hundredfold blessings will shine far into the imperial annals; thus,
though they have died, they may as well be considered living day and night.
I humbly reflect that the imperial decree is subtle and nuanced, its meaning difficult to grasp definitively.
If the Heavenly Will were uniform, then all could be made to follow it;
yet Your Majesty’s sagacious thoughts seek beyond this.
Who then would not exhaust their thoughts?
As for me, a subject of mediocre and dull wit, how could I be worthy of entrusting my words to this matter?
To regard the two teachings as non-existent—
Thus, it is revered within the sagely destiny;
since the Sage reveres it, it is not non-existent.
Therefore, we regard both teachings as existent.
Thus, one would be editing and excising during a time of clarity;
yet to excise at such a time, one fears that [the truth] may no longer exist.
This is why one hesitates at the crossroads, with the two extremes warring within.
The Way should preserve its traces, yet its principle does not satisfy the mind.
How could my narrow vision fathom the heavens, or a frog measure the ocean?
Its principle lies far beyond the reach of mere approximation.
This matter transcends the realm of intellectual knowledge;
one should naturally set aside the lead pencil and lay down the brush, withdrawing into silence and extinguishing all sound.
Yet you wish to dwell like a bird while following a fixed program of speech, or to steal a puff upon the pipes amidst the orchestra.
It shall cause those with deaf ears to listen and harmonize their customs,
and those with blind eyes to see and equalize their elders;
though there may be exhaustion within the spirit and mind.
In the end, it never reaches the realm of hearing or seeing;
it is simply that as the eight winds blow far and wide,
the myriad pipes all contribute their sounds.
When the two luminaries ascend in brilliance,
the myriad forms do not conceal their shadows; here,
we gaze longingly at their traces, hoping to follow their turning wheel.
I turn my heart toward the sun like the heliotrope and offer my service like dew to the passing station;
yet, with a face that blushes in shame, I tread upon thin ice in summer and spring,
my sense of trepidation being already extreme.
Respect and fear are intertwined. We respectfully submit this deliberation.

Liu Xiangdao, Minister of Justice and Grand Master of Ceremonies; Liu Xiangdao, Minister of Justice and Grand Master of Ceremonies, humbly considers that in the ordering of the court, solemnity and reverence must take precedence.
In the debt of gratitude for procreation, filial care through physical service is paramount;
yet now, both the teachings of Śākyamuni and Laozi have entirely reversed this,
treating even emperors and kings with an equal manner of ritual.
He has been honored by his parents,
who have shown him great forbearance from ancient times until the present day;
tracing the source of this profound outcome, there is indeed a reason why it is so.
It is surely because shaving the head differs from wearing the ceremonial cap and robes;
the *kāṣāya* holds no value as official insignia.
Therefore, having left the household life, one receives no reverence from family members.
Having renounced the secular world, how could one be constrained by the rituals of the imperial court?

As for the profound teachings of the Mysterious School, their purity and emptiness and the far-reaching influence of its Way are such that those who hold these matters in high esteem do not bow before kings or lords.
"A sovereign has those whom he does not treat as subjects;
this is precisely what that refers to.
Since the state preserves his Way, he does not bend his person."
We respectfully propose that this be accorded in accordance with the preceding chapter, so as not to violate established precedent.
Thus we deliberate.
Regarding those who prostrate: [text follows].
It is clear that a śramaṇa ought to perform prostrations.
In the past, when the Awakened Sovereign ruled the realm, he even opened the source for both faith and slander;
how much more so now, at the end of the Age of Images, that the discussion of broad and concise principles has not spread?
Recently, because the ocean of the Dharma is vast and expansive, those of similar inclinations have been difficult to distinguish, thereby defiling the profound principles;
this has become widely known at court,
leading to scholars who are bound by the literal letter of the texts [to fall into error].
To abandon the Way and follow man—
when weighed against this standard—
it cannot yet be called a grand proclamation of universal principles.
This is why I have examined various historical records and offered my criticisms accordingly;
it is my hope that those gentlemen who revere the Buddha may be able to examine this in detail.

A Memorandum on the Shamans and the Joint Petition for Prostration, in Three Parts. A Memorandum by Cui Andu, Chief Clerk of the Left Commandery of the Imperial Guard, and Shen Xuanming, Registrar, et al.: We humbly observe that when the purple vapor ascends, it manifests the True.
The wind of the Mysterious Female spread westward;
the white rainbow sank into transformation.
The essence of Nirvana flowed eastward.
The reins gallop through the clouds;
its shadow hovers over the royal capital, concentrating manifold wonders.
Its ferry of compassion illuminates the stillness.
Opening the golden garden to harmonize with the Ultimate Way,
its meaning surpasses both emptiness and existence,
while its principle penetrates the realm beyond perception and sound.
Dispelling the dust of ignorance and purifying the accumulation of karmic causes, the divine way supplements the teachings; herein there is manifest proof.
Having already followed these level tracks, one proceeds accordingly.

The corruption of traditions requires correction through reform; to criticize by saying one "strictly observes the law" while regarding high-mindedness as a "corruption," or to call it "reform" when it involves violating the scriptures to conform to secular customs—this may be acceptable regarding the specific matter at hand, but what can be said for the underlying principle? To trace its origin, we find that the reverence shown toward those in the three positions of authority is established throughout the six ranks of society.
It establishes the majestic distinction between the high and the low;
it is the root of a hundred virtues and the source of the Four Beginnings.
It proclaims the discourse on the infinite debt of gratitude owed to one's parents.
Only when the foundation is established does the Way arise;
it is here that reverence manifests and ritual becomes harmonious.
This is truly the beginning of the king’s transformation of the world.
This is the fundamental principle of heaven and earth.
The Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher;
the Emperor takes Heaven as his model.
Within this realm there are four great entities, and the King occupies one of them.
Since the Way of the King is already equal in stature,
the laws of Heaven are naturally unified within it.
As one who is a vessel for the Dharma, the Dharma alone is the root of the Way.
Those in yellow caps yearn for the Way, while those in black robes serve the Buddha.
To pay reverence to the sovereign and father is a subtle resonance with the profound waves; thus he remarked:
The Buddha-dharma is the most honored beyond the world;
the Emperor is the greatest within the realm.
Yet, while the teachings remain, he is compelled to submit and yield.
To remain unrestrained is akin to being categorized among the common masses;
this is for the waters of the Dharma to be dammed and fail to flow.
How could there be such a profound resonance with the mysterious waves? Moreover, as soon as the records of the precepts are elevated, [the transgressions] are revealed.

If even those of the lowest status are utterly reverent in their prostrations, how much more so for those of noble rank whose social distance is vast? To suddenly abandon respect by refusing to bend the knee is a grave error.
Wang Mi said: [as quoted above].
As for why śramaṇas respect one another regardless of seniority and exchange formal greetings,
it is because those who dwell in the imperial palace recognize that when the fundamental purpose is the same, the order of elders and juniors is established; yet,
when there is a separation in their paths, there is no obligation to yield or bow down.
Truly profound are these words;

they may serve as a mirror for reflection. One must surely go alone into the mountain forests, forgetting both self and others, blending together the near and the distant, and equalizing honor and disgrace.
To bestow favor upon me would not be for this purpose;
to diminish oneself—how could that be called wrong?
One should naturally become as if devoid of emotion.
Profoundly still and eternally tranquil,
he bowed his head in reverence toward Kapilavastu and performed a formal prostration upon beholding the World-Honored One.
His dusty appearance was no different from that of the laity, yet his reverence did not deviate from the truth. Tandan said:
"A śramaṇa sheds his finery and dons black robes."
The distinction between the monastic and the secular is vast, yet you pay obeisance in a manner that contradicts the Buddha’s teachings.
Although you cite the scriptural texts in detail,
your claim that "reverence does not deviate from the truth" and that "the physical form is no different from the laity" is untenable.
This is to take south as north and turn white into black;
yet, Lord Boyang [Laozi] provided his instructions by blending with the light,
and Puji [Huisi] expounded the teachings through ordinary etiquette.
The virtue of Miaoye was humble and respectful,
far conforming to the regulations of mutual illumination; Boyang was born in the Zhou dynasty of the Ji clan,
his person serving as the Recorder of the Pillar.
To serve as an official is one of the duties of the royal court;
to be a follower of the Confucian tradition that emphasizes the Way is one of its schools. Therefore, it is only natural that they prostrate before their sovereign and parents.
As for the rite of not bowing lightly, this is merely a temporary expedient for the fourfold assembly.
This is like when Wenming entered the customs of the naked tribes and discarded his robes;
it cannot be taken as a model for all the lands under heaven. Furthermore, among the three realms of existence, the human realm occupies the lowest position.
If the branches still extend respect, how can the root be doubted? [Hui]tan replied:
"This is why the monastic community respects one another as teacher and disciple."
It is precisely because the teachings and their meanings are not different;
it is not a matter of speaking in terms of origin and manifestation.
How can you be so reckless? If you were to consider the *kāṣāya* robe as different from the dragon-patterned robes of the nobility, [you would be mistaken].
The *hu* silk headcloth is distinct from the *bi* feathered cap;
since the attire is already martial,
why must the prostration be elaborate?
Each followed their own fundamental nature without deviating from the standard of propriety.

There were those whose long-standing conduct was upright and reclusive, whose pure regulations stirred the world, whose spiritual transformations resonated like echoes, and whose observance of precepts was diligent and arduous—
refined as the *tóng* and *luán* birds and as pure as the cranes in the azure heavens.
With embroidered banners summoning beasts and jade talismans commanding spirits,
his virtue is refined and his years advanced; thus,
he is exempted from the rites of prostration.
As for the rest—those who are beginners and those of later generations—their voices have fallen silent;
let them all instead show full reverence toward their sovereign and father.
I request that this be immediately codified as a permanent law. [The Emperor] rebuked him, saying:
If not bowing is considered wrong,
then how could it be appropriate to exempt those of virtuous character and advanced age?
If not bowing is considered right, [then why this distinction?]
Thus, it would be inappropriate to require juniors and beginners to prostrate, as such contradictory advances and retreats would lead to mutual discord.
I request that this be immediately codified into the permanent regulations.
What shortcoming have you observed? In this way, one may advance in virtue and cultivate their practice.
The path of transcending the mundane flourished ever more;
those of austere discipline took refuge upon the altar,
and their resolve to enter the Way became increasingly ardent.

Chapter Fourteen: The Gate of Suffering Within the Three Realms. Now, the prison of the three realms revolves on four sides.
Whether laypeople or monastics, as long as they have not severed the delusion of a self, none can escape;
being thus entangled by birth and death, they remain bound.
The body and mind are subject to exhaustion and ceaseless transformation;
there is nothing that is not suffering.
Thus, the Sūtra says:

The three realms are entirely suffering; what is there to enjoy? Yet sentient beings are constantly deluded, claiming that the world is permanent and pleasurable, while the causes of supramundane bliss are impermanent and suffering.
How can one be so deeply immersed in this state of such utter perversion?
As soon as one tests piercing the body, one immediately perceives painful sensation;
how then can it be called pleasure?
I shall briefly cite several passages as evidence that [existence] is nothing but suffering.
If one were to claim that food and drink constitute pleasure,
then one should experience harmony of body and joy of mind whenever one consumes them in abundance.
For what reason does even a slight deviation from the proper measure become a source of affliction?
If one considers clothing to be a pleasure,
then one should wear only a single garment throughout spring and summer, with a heart of loving-kindness free from satiety.
What is the meaning of wearing different clothing according to the cold and heat?
It clarifies that one does not find pleasure in worldly enjoyments, for this is the root of suffering.
If you claim that dwellings constitute pleasure, [it is not so].
For what reason does the mind not remain in one place?
Since it is driven to constant movement,
we clearly know that it seeks to avoid suffering.
If one considers one's wife, children, and kinsmen to be sources of happiness,
then they should always be singing and laughing;
for what reason do they suddenly wail in grief when faced with impermanence?
One should know that being choked with grief reveals that one's kin are truly the root of suffering.
If one were to consider exquisite beauty as pleasure,
then it ought to bring perpetual delight to the eyes and mind, and forever comfort the physical form.
For what reason does one's countenance change in an instant, with hair turning white and face turning dark, bringing grief and pain to the youthful splendor of beauty?
Thus we know that this form is inherently suffering.
It does not come from outside.
If one were to consider pleasant sounds as pleasure,
then one should never tire of watching and listening when strings and flutes play in profusion.
What is the meaning of this? That one becomes drowsy and weary at a young age and finds no pleasure in hearing [the Dharma]—one should know that this is suffering.
If one considers the indulgence in wine to be pleasure, [it is not so].
One ought to find contentment, dispel sorrow, and remain forever free from affliction and suffering;
why then is the spirit clouded, the mind distressed, and the joints and bones so painfully aching?
Or perhaps, because of this matter, one will be subjected to flogging, caning, or imprisonment.
They lose their bodies and meet untimely deaths; they ruin their families and bring ruin to their nations, suffering immeasurable pain.
If one considers companionship and socializing to be pleasure, [one is mistaken].
In that case, one ought to roam and disport oneself all day long without knowing weariness;

If one were to claim that lewdness is pleasure,

Why is it that when one indulges the mind and gives rein to desire, one immediately becomes exhausted and weary?
The brain is drained and the marrow extracted; the head reels and the eyes grow dim;

The mouth becomes parched and the lips wither, while the four limbs tremble;

One should know that lewdness is truly the root of suffering.
If one were to claim that honor and position constitute happiness,

The above points have been stated in general terms;

The three realms of the world are entirely a mass of suffering;

I pay homage to the entire Sangha Jewel of the ten directions.
I pay homage to the future Buddha Maitreya Bodhisattva and his assembly in the Tuṣita Heaven, who shall descend to be born hereafter.
Homage to the wandering great being, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Saṃgha.
Homage to the great being who rescues from suffering, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Saṃgha.
Homage to the great being who protects the Dharma, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva Saṃgha.
Homage to the Sangha of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, the Great Being who extinguishes transgressions.
Homage to the Sangha of all Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions who practice the great mind of the Way.
Homage to the Sangha of all Pratyekabuddhas throughout the ten directions who practice the mind of a Pratyekabuddha.
Homage to all the śrāvaka saṃghas throughout the ten directions who practice the inferior vehicle.
Homage to the śrāvaka saṃgha headed by Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, who shall abide in the Dharma for ten thousand years.
Homage to the sons of the Buddha, the śrāvaka saṅgha residing at Louhuluo for ten thousand years.
Homage to the śrāvaka saṅgha residing in the mountains and seas of Shan Prefecture for ninety million times ten thousand years.
I pay homage to all the ordinary and noble Saṃghas currently present within the three thousandfold world system.
May all sentient beings always share the same vehicle with the worthy and holy ones upon the Right Path;
may they open their wisdom and generate merit, never falling into the evil realms.
In every birth, one encounters virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
by subduing and eliminating afflictions (*kleśa*), one attains liberation from all states of existence (*bhava*).
[This is] a verse on the Sangha-gate; the five jewels have already been moistened, and through discourse, faith arises.
Though the eight cassias may be fragrant, it is their fragrance that defines their character;
these wondrous principles and ultimate words are the treasures of the sages.
Were it not for such a person, who could propagate the Way?
Illuminating emptiness through contemplative methods, I observe the flux of consciousness;
consoling the worldly and gazing upon the common folk, I weary of birth and old age.
I sever emotional attachments and cut off all joy and delight.
Though one may fall from noble glory and abandon ornate refinement,
loved ones vanish in an instant like wind-blown mist;
wealth and profit drift aimlessly like dust upon the grass.
Measured against the dragon and the clouds, how could one call this lofty?
Washing one's feet at the Yangtze and Han rivers, one feels even more ashamed before the bright [moon].
28. Exhorting the Monks to Enter the Gate. Exhorting the Monks to Enter the Gate, Number Twenty-Eight. Regarding "exhortation": [it refers to] urging [the monks to enter].
This is the height of earnest sincerity.
From the arousal of such earnest sincerity,
the sentiment of wishing for goodness becomes profound.
Therefore, regarding every subtle and minute virtue,
one must earnestly exhort and entreat others to increase and give rise to the practice of wisdom.
It must not be abandoned midway.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of exhortation:
exhorting sentient beings to practice the precepts and wholesome deeds, thereby perfecting the roots of all virtues.
I exhort all Buddhas to protect and deliver sentient beings and to cause the teaching of the Dharma to endure for a long time.
Throughout the ten directions, in the four evil realms,
I now universally entreat them to cultivate and maintain all the practices of the precepts.
Having obtained this human body,
I now exhort all people throughout the ten directions.
Causing them to cultivate the ten wholesome actions so that they may be born in the heavens;
the devas and humans of the ten directions—
I now exhort you all to ascend and establish yourselves in the stage of right determination,
so that you may be freed from the evil realms.
I now exhort all those who are training throughout the ten directions:
awaken and examine all afflictions.
May they swiftly realize the stage of no-more-learning.
I now exhort all the Arhats of the ten directions.
Knowing that this is not the ultimate stage,
there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle;
even the pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions [are included therein].
I now exhort you all to accomplish the wisdom of great compassion and to teach and transform all sentient beings.
I now exhort the multitudes of humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles to realize the Tathāgatagarbha within their own bodies.
I now exhort all bodhisattvas who are practicing the bodhisattva conduct.
Practicing the ten perfections,
one swiftly ascends the ten stages;
such is the bodhisattva of Tuṣita Heaven.
I now exhort you all:
constantly turn the wheel of non-retrogression and swiftly descend to deliver all living beings.
The wisdom of the Bodhisattvas is not yet clear;
I now exhort them all.
O Vajra, who extinguishes the burden of defilements!
Revealing the true nature:
all Buddhas of the ten directions who have first attained perfect enlightenment.
I entreat you to turn the wheel of Dharma for the peace and happiness of all sentient beings;
may all Buddhas of the ten directions likewise do so.
If you wish to relinquish your life-span,
I now take refuge and entreat you:
may you remain long in this world.
Thus, I now exhort all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to give rise to this earnest resolve.
Therefore, I bow my head in prostration.
Verse of the Gate of Exhortation: "Waiting for the Yellow River to clear, I encounter this Sage Dynasty;
may divine wisdom look down from afar to receive me."
The white sun races its light, yet it does not shed its radiance upon me;
the humble aspirations of the sunflower and the mugwort merely lean and yearn toward it.
Filling all of space and existence, it pervades the entirety of the three realms.
Cotton wool fills the universe and exhausts the eight expanses;
with the light of virtue and his deeds accomplished, he ascends to supreme enlightenment.
In silent stillness he abides eternally, alone able to transcend.
Scorched by the fires of desire, I long for the clouds and dew;
submerged in the waters of affliction, I look toward the boat and the bridge.
Your vast compassion and universal deliverance were pledged of old.

They harbor abundant and predominant thoughts of envy; therefore,
when they see others practicing virtue, they give rise to malicious intentions,
seeking to destroy and ruin their efforts so that they do not reach fulfillment.
Yet that former person has not necessarily impaired their conduct;
it is this envious one who falsely increases affliction and feverish distress,
thereby increasing delusions and karma so that birth and death continue without end.
Therefore, the sage harmonizes his mind and restrains his intentions;
he practices this sympathetic joy and likewise exhorts all sentient beings to do the same.
As it has been taught, so shall they practice.
All the subtle virtues possessed by all beings throughout the ten directions—
Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom;
filial piety, nourishment, humility, and courtesy;
kindness, harmony, affection, and respect.
Their conduct is upright, pure, and clean;
if there are such virtues as these,
I now rejoice in them all.
Laypeople who have renounced desire,
reverently practice the Tathāgata’s precepts:
the three refuges and the five or eight precepts.
The ten wholesome precepts of a bodhisattva;
the purity of all disciplinary codes;
and being free from ill repute.
I now rejoice in all such merits as these:
the feeding of the Sangha and the giving of Dharma robes.
Bathing away the defilements of affliction,
they rescue and gather in all who are impoverished;
those who are famished, cold, destitute, and obstructed.
For those suffering from the hardships and perils of illness,
he performs the deed of compassionate pity by bestowing medicine;
such are his meritorious qualities.
I now rejoice in all of this:
making fine wells along desolate roads,
and providing bridges and boats to ferry people and goods across.
Gardens, groves, ponds, flowers, and fruits—
by offering these to the Buddha and providing for the Sangha,
one eliminates thirst and the affliction of heat.
The merit thereof is truly immeasurable.
All such virtues as these,
I now rejoice in with all my being.
They have established the flow of the sutras and the teachings of the Dharma;
they kindle the lamp to give rise to the clarity of wisdom,
practicing recitation and chanting.
Having definitively resolved all meanings and purposes,
if one further explains them to others,
their heart of joy will increase manifold.
I now rejoice in all such merits as these,
and in the establishment of various stūpas and temples.
Hall-temples and jeweled stupas;
murals and wooden statues;
[images] made of gold, silver, copper, stone, and so forth.
By transmitting and transcribing the various marks and signs,
one reveals the Dharma-body;
such are these merits.
I now rejoice in all of this.
If there are those who construct monasteries,
or provide beds, curtains, and bedding;
Causing those who have stilled their minds to find peace within the groves of dhyāna,
they enter and emerge from the gates of suffering and emptiness.
I now rejoice in all such merits as these, including the sequential contemplation of peaceful extinction.
The Tathāgata, with great compassion,
skillfully expounds all dharma-gates,
giving rise to the practice of sympathetic joy.
Now we practice and study,
following and rejoicing in all the śrāvakas who endure suffering to cross over birth and death.
I rejoice in all bodhisattvas who do not abandon the experience of the evil realms;
I rejoice in the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The Fearless One, Honored among Gods and Humans,
is able to draw forth all sentient beings from the prison of the three realms.
May all classes of sentient beings fully attain the Buddha-way;
for this reason, I rejoice.
I prostrate in homage to all Buddhas.
A Verse on Rejoicing: Hearing of the good is like finding a lamp or a fine book;
seeing the worthy, one thinks of emulating them—this is the beauty of the universal admonition.
His filial piety moved the spirits and shook the earth through its sincerity;
his loyalty was such that he would have sacrificed his head and shed his entrails as his principle of conduct.
He revitalized the rites and composed writings to propagate the constitutional laws.
His strategic ingenuity was as swift as a gale and his valor quelled the wicked and violent;
his clarity entered the realm of simplicity, and his will was profound and tranquil.
His lofty discourse exhausted the subtle and accords with the mysteries of the spirit.
Sacrificing one’s body to save others without seeking fame;
regarding wealth lightly and valuing righteousness without expecting recompense.
A hundred deeds and myriad virtues form a vast and diverse path.
Having finished the prayer with utmost sincerity and deep contemplation, one rejoices with exultation.
30. The Gate of Dedication to the Buddha Way (The Thirtieth). Regarding "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*):
its meaning is non-attachment.
Originally, all sentient beings have fully cultivated the myriad practices and sacrificed their bodies, lives, and wealth;
yet, the reason they are unable to attain liberation from birth and death is as follows:
All [these states] arise because of attachment to karmic fruition and the inability to relinquish it.
If one can refrain from grasping with the mind and practice the means of gathering and delivering beings, [one will be liberated].
Whenever there is even a slight merit, they dedicate it to all sentient beings so that they may turn toward the Buddha-way;
thus, they no longer give rise to attachment toward the karmic fruits of their actions,
and they become serenely liberated from birth and death.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"Practicing according to what has been taught and dedicating [the merit] constitutes great benefit."
Therefore, all virtuous deeds performed should be dedicated toward enlightenment,
while simultaneously exhorting sentient beings not to be attached to their karmic rewards.
Why is this? It is because this very physical body is the basis for karmic retribution;
throughout one's entire life, it is nourished, adorned, and embellished.
Since one must inevitably die, it is in vain to merely cling to existence.
Were it not for the darkness of ignorance, who would greedily cherish this body?
Only those with little wisdom and clarity act thus.
How could one not feel weary [of cyclic existence] at all times?
For this reason, when the wise person presses their chest and reflects upon their own mind,
they find no room for greedy attachment that would cause them to revolve within the cycle of birth and death.
The subtle roots of goodness practiced by all sentient beings throughout the ten directions— namely,
benevolence, filial piety, humility, and respect.
Compassionate, loving, gentle, and so forth;
loyal, upright, practicing propriety and wisdom;
showing pity and providing relief to the orphaned and the destitute.
In this way, all mundane virtues are dedicated toward the Buddha-way;
[so too are] all those of the various non-Buddhist paths.
They engaged in various arduous ascetic practices:
scorching their bodies with the five fires,
leaping from cliffs, and casting themselves into water and fire.
The practice of self-binding, smearing ashes,
and so forth— all these immeasurable wrong views are now dedicated for the sake of turning away from them.
All shall return to the path of perfect enlightenment;
all lay followers of pure faith shall take refuge in the precepts and practice the ten wholesome deeds.
Even all women are able to cultivate merit and are also able to skillfully expound the Dharma.
I cultivate all manner of wondrous merits and dedicate them to all living beings,
that we may together realize the unsurpassed path.
All the assembly of disciples,
upon hearing his voice, immediately attained realization;
"Welcome," he said, and they became bhikṣus.
Up to the four fruits of the path;
the skillful means and the initial contemplation consist of the perceptions of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
I also dedicate these merits to all sentient beings,
that we may together proceed toward the unsurpassed path.
To all the Pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions...
They naturally become pratyekabuddhas;
having deeply awakened in another life,
they clearly understand the law of causes and conditions.
Appearing and disappearing to transform sentient beings,
dwelling alone in the joy of sublime tranquility—
thus he encompasses all.
Dedicating it all toward the Buddha-way,
the bodhisattvas of the ten directions read and recite the sutras and dharmas.
Regarding "entering and emerging from dhyāna":
it is to exhort sentient beings to practice the various kinds of good deeds;
such are the three types of goodness.
All roots of every virtue are likewise dedicated to all sentient beings,
as they turn toward the unsurpassed path.
Regarding all virtues and so forth,
up to the fruits of the noble ones,
one has not yet exhausted the understanding of emptiness.
Existence and non-existence are both exhausted;
may all beings together enter the truly wondrous realm.
If they turn their minds that possess signs toward the path of liberation,
such are the bodhisattvas.
I now exhort you to dedicate [your merit] and give rise to this mind free from attachment;
for this reason, I prostrate in homage.
Verses on the Gate of Dedication: Vast and distant, the nine lands each have different forms;
Chaos and turmoil, the four secular realms possess manifold dispositions.
Driving chariots and feeding horses, one pursues worldly occupations.
In the marketplace, they trade righteousness and peddle empty fame;
the three schools of Mohism are in chaotic conflict and do not accord,
while the seven masters of Confucianism remain muddled and never unified.
Auspiciousness and misfortune, as well as prohibitions and constraints, are merely matters of numerology and technique;
acquisition and loss, separation and union, are truly纵横 (zōnghéng—transverse and vertical, i.e., manifold and pervasive).
As for the morning sun and evening moon, what can ultimately be gained from them?
To throw oneself from a cliff or rush into fire is to waste one's life in vain.
Alas! Having lost the Way, you now turn your chariot back;
follow that flowing water toward the eastern sea.
31. The Chapter on the Adornment of Making Vows. Regarding the thirty-first chapter, "The Adornment of Making Vows":
All destinations resulting from various evils are conditioned by greed, hatred, and delusion within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
Nothing exceeds these in terms of harming oneself and others;
therefore, the sutras designate them as the "three fundamental poisons.
They are capable of afflicting and vexing, agitating both body and mind.
Regarding the three groups of three and the nine types within the unwholesome dependent origination,
these nine meanings apply to both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
those arising from the three wholesome roots are called wholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*).
The arising of the three unwholesome roots is called an evil path of action.
Therefore, the practitioner should always unify the mind and not allow it to be disturbed;
should even a subtle sign of agitation arise, they must immediately become aware of it.
Guard the six sense faculties so they are not defiled by sensory objects;
constantly make great vows to adorn yourself.
May all sentient beings, from this very day until they reach enlightenment, [be likewise adorned].
One's eyes should never gaze upon the forms of lustful and lewd seducers;
nor should one gaze upon the forms of those who are wrathful and hideous, or those who are cruel, foolish, dull-witted, arrogant, or heterodox.
I vow to behold the color of the eternally abiding Dharma-body throughout all ten directions;
the color of the eight manifestations of the Bodhisattva’s descent into birth;
and the color of the Tathāgata’s marks and signs, gathered together in the harmonious assembly of the noble multitude.
May all sentient beings never hear the sounds of lamentation and sorrowful sighing, the cries of suffering in the hells,
the voices of those enduring pain as hungry ghosts or animals,
or the clamor of the eightfold sufferings confronting one another.
May the sounds of the four hundred and four diseases arise;
may the sounds of the eighty-four thousand afflictions arise;
and may my ears always hear the eightfold melodic voices of all Buddhas preaching the Dharma.
The sounds of the eighty-four thousand pāramitās;
the sounds of the fruits of the three vehicles, the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and their various merits—
may all sentient beings never smell with their noses the scent of food that has the flavor of killing.
The thirty-six substances are the breath within this leather bag;
they give rise to the scent of fine silks and fragrant unguents,
while the five pungent herbs can permeate the nine stages of the corpse’s putrid stench.
May my nose always smell the fragrance of all trees, grasses, and woods throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
the fragrance of the merits of the five precepts, the eight precepts, the ten wholesome paths, and the six recollections;
and the fragrance of the untainted perfections—the ten stages, the five factors of liberation, the ten powers, and the eighty-four thousand [dharmas]—of those in training and those beyond training.
May the fragrance of the Dharma preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions cause all sentient beings’ tongues never again to taste the mixed flavors of the flesh and lives of other beings,
which give rise to the savor of afflictions.
May the tongue always taste the immortal flavor of nectar.
May the natural food of the heavens, upon reaching the root of the tongue, transform into the supreme flavor—
the very flavor consumed by all Buddhas.

May all sentient beings never experience the sensation of desire born from the subtle touch of sexual misconduct, even while their bodies are unaware of it; [may they instead] savor the taste of the joy of Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna, and attain the most supreme and excellent flavor of liberation and nirvāṇa.
They do not perceive the touch of the boiling cauldrons and icy waters;
nor the touches of the various sufferings of hungry ghosts and animals;
nor the touches of the four hundred and four diseases, of cold and heat, wind and frost, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, lice, hunger, thirst, and the afflictions of hardship.
May my body always be conscious, cool, and robust; may my mind awaken to peace and security, realize the Way, and attain the eightfold mastery of flight and touch.
May all sentient beings, from this day until they reach Bodhi, [attain these same qualities].
The mind constantly perceives and understands the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
the eighty-four thousand dharmas of affliction (*kleśa*),
and the ten evil deeds and five heinous crimes.
The ninety-six kinds of heterodox teachers' doctrines,
the three miserable realms to be loathed, and the great suffering of birth and death—
may I always wish to know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The Buddha is the King of Physicians;
the Dharma is the excellent medicine;
and the Sangha is the caregiver.
He treats the afflictions of birth and death for all sentient beings,
causing them to attain liberation;
his mind is always unimpeded.
Untainted by either emptiness or existence, this verse on the gateway of making vows describes what the mind aspires to: that distant shore.
Why linger long in the affairs of the floating mundane world? Let us illuminate with the sun of wisdom and mount the clouds of Dharma.
Ascending the perilous city, one emerges from the dusty halls;
fragrant pearls blaze forth as the seasons turn,
and jeweled trees sway, awakening both dusk and dawn.
The pure dew gathers its sweetness for eternal sipping;
the garden’s radiance flows forth as a constant delight.
There is no need to wait for the sacrificial cauldrons of King Yin or the delicacies of a square-foot banquet.
What use is the Qin zither plucked by slender fingers?
Let your diligent sincerity and earnest vows remain forever unchanging.
From this moment forth, resist the suffering of worldly toil.

He loosed the sharp arrows of liberating wisdom;
his war-horse neighed with vigor and his light steps were majestic.
He stroked his sword and brandished his flying spear.
I chant this long poem to summon my adversary:
the General’s family has enjoyed successive generations of illustrious glory;
he has rectified and sustained the imperial enterprise and served the sacred court throughout his career.
There has never been any deficiency.
His nobility was such that he was a Dharma teacher to Śāriputra and his five hundred disciples;
he possessed profound insight into the mandate of Heaven.
Having received the transformative influence of the King,
they opened their hearts to the Holy Sovereign;
all were granted titles, ranks, enfeoffments, and rewards, with lands bestowed such that their merit equaled that of the veteran ministers of old.
His fame covers the ten thousand regions;
yet what is in your heart that you have so recklessly given rise to heterodox views,
remaining haughty and defiant in these remote frontiers while stubbornly clinging to your ordinary status?
Poisonous harm breaks forth among the common people,
and calamities flow through eternal kalpas;
how lamentable this is!
How could this not be without error?
Formerly, when times were chaotic, you were deluded by external things and fell into madness;
your mind surrendered to falsehood and fled outward.
Even the wise and accomplished may long lose their way through a single transgression among a hundred virtues;
this refers to Your Majesty who, having grasped wisdom, returned to folly.
You have attributed the blame to the imperial gate tower, bound yourself, and withdrawn your hairpin.
I have traveled with a group of eminent scholars, finding delight in the Way throughout our lives;
yet, from beginning to end,
I have maintained my humble nature and persisted in my delusions.
Seeking comfort in a false position,
they rely on the mountain of delusion to elevate themselves and depend upon the forest of views to exercise their thoughts.
They indulge in the defiled dust of the six desires and revel in perverse delusions to gratify their natures,
erecting the lofty banner of arrogance.
He arrayed the malevolent ranks of ignorance,
strode boldly upon the long path, and recklessly toyed with the divine instruments of power;
he usurped the celestial palace and defied the sun and moon.
I fear it is no different from raising one's hand to block the three luminaries,
or digging up soil to fill the four seas,
or beating a drum to compete with the sound of thunder.
To strive to compete with the brilliance of fire is like setting one's mind upon an empty standard;
though the intention is noble, the task is difficult to accomplish.
Nevertheless, you, General, have cultivated virtue at the profound ford.
Originally inheriting from Mi Yuan,
his brilliance shone forth so brilliantly that all subordinates gazed upon him;
the foundation for attaining noble status was easily ascended.
The achievements of your past are truly regrettable;
you should reform your ways and cultivate the future, turning over a new leaf to submit in allegiance.
Apologize for your transgressions at the Imperial Gate and align yourself with the Way through friendship.
When both family and state endure together, and both ruler and subject attain distinction;
when one gains renown and secures peace, with clear vision and profound insight,
and one's kin and followers live in tranquility— can this not be called beautiful?
The Great Master raised his voice across the myriad regions like a flash of lightning;
he held the Dharma-conch in his hand and leveled the sword of wisdom.
The blade of the Way shone brilliantly as he led the vanguard.
The numinous drums resound their tones from the rear ranks;
a single strike of the divine bell causes the ten directions to collapse,
and as the ocean waves surge with flying billows, the dry lands boil like a cauldron.
At that time, Mount Sumeru will be reduced to fine dust,
and heaven and earth will revolve as a single grain of millet.
Immovability rests upon the left lapel;
wondrous bliss is held in the right palm.
Such is his supernormal power.
How could this be appropriate?
Nevertheless, our Dharma King, embodying great benevolence and compassion,
does not wish to strike immediately.
He temporarily halted his various armies and briefly reined in his divine chariot.
On the road, he dispatched a letter,
hoping to turn back those who were following the path of delusion.
You should quickly determine a sound plan:
bind yourself with your face to the ground and return to the capital, surrendering your life at the royal court;
only then, in leisurely seclusion, will you be fit for the duties of governance.
If it were not for you, whom else could it be?
For the sage possesses supreme wisdom and discerns the subtle movements of fate;
he clearly understands the gravity of his responsibility and strives to avoid calamity.
To reach the limit and know how to return is what the gentleman prizes;
this is indeed the high autumn of transforming fortune.
This is the excellent standard for assessing merit.
In the past, King Jie of Xia was unrighteous, and the King of Yin launched a punitive expedition against him;
Zhou Shou of Shang initiated disorder, and Duke Wu of Zhou established his army.
This is the constant rule of antiquity and the present;
it is the clear admonition of the General.
Although we may be separated in form from one another in these times, [our bond remains].
The wind flows through the flavor of the Way;
though humans and devas may tread upon treacherous paths,
how could they suffice to create a sense of separation?
I have thus suddenly surrendered my life in accordance with your letter;
for this reason, I deeply lament the earnestness and detail of your words.
Regarding those who passed away long ago, I do not wish to allow their fragrant orchids to wither in summer nor their verdant branches to break off their tips.
Reflect deeply on these ultimate words and follow well this excellent counsel.
Do not allow your person to fall into the three calamities;
do not allow the six heavens to grow only wild oats and weeds.
As Xunmu gazes upward, his emotions are further relieved and unburdened.
With many thoughts upon reaching the paper,
my writing fails to fully express my meaning.
Shi Dao’an bows his head.
Proclamation from the Lord of Māras! Proclamation from the Lord of Māras! To the Kingdom of the Great Dream, the Prefecture of the Long Night.
Unaware of the prefecture,
one utters delirious speech in the village;
such is the sovereign lord of the six realms, the Emperor of Paranirmita-vaśavartin.

This report and proclamation are addressed to the Honorable An Dharma Master, Minister of Buddha Affairs and Great General of the Southern Jambudvīpa, Commissioner for the Pacification of the Way, at your esteemed station.
Having received news from afar, we rejoice at this brief encounter.
Having examined the phrasing and flavor of your words, I am truly delighted.
Only now do I see that the ministers of this great kingdom possess lofty standards of ritual and righteousness.
I have heard that you, General, are humble and magnanimous in heart, while your secret conduct is profound and mysterious.
With mountains and rivers as its girdle, it encompasses the universe;
its concerns for the ancestral temple are profound, and its anxieties extend to the common people.
Its refined spirit rises ten thousand fathoms high, and its true heart towers ten thousand cubits tall.
Truly, he is the sturdy grass tested by a fierce wind;
a loyal minister in an age of chaos.
I hope that we may encounter one another on the road as neighbors.
We are not separated by distance;
humbly following the ways of human affairs, I have composed this brief reply.
Formerly, when the House of Zhou had declined and the six states were in turmoil like boiling water, [the world was divided].
The mandate of the Han dynasty was extinguished and the realm was divided into three parts.
Sometimes foreign barbarians invaded and rebelled, spreading their poison across the Central Plains;
at other times, internal calamities arose in secret, bringing disaster upon the virtuous and good.
The magpie rising at its appointed time and the leopard changing its stripes when the occasion arises have occurred since antiquity;
how could it be limited to the present day alone?
Alas! As the common people have accumulated sins, Heaven has sent down calamity.
Emperor Śākya has suddenly ascended to the beyond;
grief envelops us ministers and subjects, and sorrow permeates all within the realm.
The Crown Prince Maitreya nurtured his virtue within the Mind Palace;
when the full moon paused upon the mountain, he remained hidden among the deep thickets like a medicinal herb.
Thus did the age of the hundred-six calamities unfold.
In our time, the position of the九五 (Jiǔwǔ) sovereign has been deficient;
the feudal lords are treacherous, sly, and suspicious as they dwell together;
and the regulations and tracks of the eighteen divisions are inconsistent and divergent.
The ninety-six heterodox paths intermingle like sacrificial vessels and stands;
wolves howl along the seashore and owls hoot in mountain coves.
To the left, they do not record words; to the right, they do not record events.
The national constitution and court statutes wither away like frost and dew;
the celestial seals and imperial jade vessels [lie desolate].
Like ice melting and leaves scattering, the ministers resent and the people are incensed; the multitudes rebel and kinsmen desert.
They flee with no place of return, wandering aimlessly and departing forever.
I humbly submit that while some belong to an era of great peace, bathing in the transforming influence of the court,
others encounter a world of chaos, seeking to bring relief amidst the turmoil of war;
this is precisely the exercise of expedient means by those of universal understanding.
I respectfully lead this army of righteousness, exerting myself so fervently that I forget to eat.
I ascend mountains to subdue tigers and stand by rivers to slay dragons;
I weave together arms and letters, regarding my own person lightly while valuing righteousness above all.
The altars of the state and the grain are not what I contemplate;
the celestial throne is not what I aspire to.
It is simply that my mind-city has no sovereign, and I am distracted by the delusions of worldly toil.
The flow of the *tadāmbara* (the realm of desire) extends far together with the source of the mind; the vast,
hazy dream lasts as long as the eternal night.
Furthermore, while resting briefly to console the people and punish the guilty,
he first dispatched General Foam-Bubble, Duke Huang Xuanhou,
leading troops of Empty Flowers.
He spurred on horses of mirage and took his position at the corner of a celestial city;
he arrayed his troops in an order of floating clouds.
The spears and armor gleamed brightly, and bows and halberds were arrayed in ranks;
before the blades had even crossed, the enemy forces were already defeated.
Next, he commanded General Jianxiang Sizhugong.
Leading the multitude of the *gong* and *shang* notes,
they occupy the valley where sounds are transmitted;
as each sound is heard, it is immediately excised.
Next, he commanded Lan-xie-bo, the Great General of the Hundred Harmonies,
to lead the army of fragrances;
riding upon the wind, they deployed their ranks so that for a thousand li there was not a cloud.
Next, he commanded the Great General of the Six Tastes to lead his troops of succulent delicacies as the Commander-in-Chief of the Gate of the Face.
He guarded the mouth of the vast ocean,
devouring everything without exception.
Next, he commanded the Great General of the Seven Touches.
Leading a host of fine and smooth [warriors],
as soon as the battle drums were struck, his body-city crumbled away.
When his five armies went forth to attack, they were constantly victorious in a hundred battles.
Heaven has bestowed its protection upon us, so that nothing is unsuitable.
Fearing that my investigation of his lair was not exhaustive, I have personally set out to demand his punishment.
Now that my martial robes are donned, he shall emerge from his hollow den.
They unleash wisdom from its deep spring and stir the majesty of mountains and peaks,
yet they must still confront the armies of deluded thoughts.
Their number exceeds ten million;
they all have submerged their spiritual consciousness within the ocean and concealed their shadows upon the mountain of the mind.
Their generals and commanders now take up their swords at the frontier passes.
The conscripted soldiers brandished their blades and formed battle arrays;
they lined the void and blocked the distant reaches like soaring smoke and gathering mist,
none of whom lacked a heroic spirit that pierced the heavens.
Vast clouds of falsehood are disgorged at the limit of reality,
where a lofty wind strikes the earth;
the waves of delusive dust are stirred upon the ocean of intrinsic nature.
Striking at the ranks of the army of the Way,
they shed their husks in a frosty night;
once the single mind has perished, the distance to returning to the source becomes ever more remote.
The six cravings have already become like a dwelling fire that blazes ever more fiercely;
they sweep across and plunder from all sides, attacking from front and back.
The six extraordinary maneuvers and three secret strategies are first stored within his breast.
Within a hundred paces, a thousand honors were achieved without the need for a frontal array;
thus, like clouds dispersing and mist rolling away,
my Way flourished.
Thereupon, offices were divided and positions established to implement my governance and transformation.
I commanded the General of the Household, the Marquis of Lian, to crouch like a tiger upon Mount Tan.
General Xingse is as parsimonious as a dragon coiled within the sea;
those who look to him for relief find no harbor on either land or water.
By imperial decree, he is bound as a *dili* general.
The storehouses of yin and yang are established;
the dust of emotion attaches to the horse as one observes the union of husband and wife.
The waters of craving flow for a time, drenching the city of the body.
As soon as the fire of desire flares up, the celestial temple is consumed by flames;
General Shenxing has already perished in the burning waters.
By imperial decree, the fierce Calvary is ordered to keep their bows and swords at the ready.
With poison and venom, they brandish halberds and spears in their hands;
with stern and formidable soldiers, they guard the fortified city of bribes,
causing General Pingfen to vanish his voice and erase his traces.
By Imperial Decree, the Censor-in-Chief for Rectitude is ordered to suspend his surveillance.
The Martial Protector of the Underlying Tendencies shall follow and stabilize the imperial governance.
Abandoning the dissipation of ignorance and ceasing all arbitrary indulgence, one awaits the realization of the conditioned.
May the single horse of diligence be made to gallop upon the fourfold path of exertion;
may the two arrows of Kāla [be drawn].
He does not shoot at the three gates of emptiness;
the valiant general causes the winds and smoke to subside.
By imperial decree, the Grand Marshal of Applied Thought and Observation establishes his headquarters in the First Dhyāna.
With wrong thoughts acting as generals, they array their ranks within the three realms of existence.
The source of the mind, failing to achieve stillness, is repeatedly buffeted by wind and waves;
the branches of dhyāna, wishing to flourish, once again encounter frost and snow.
General Anjing lies buried amidst the chaotic realm.
By imperial decree, I have come to see Gaotunana Ridge,
where ten thousand blades of delusive mountains rise and a hundredfold lines of suspicious fortifications stand.
I have returned from the wilderness to seek the path to the celestial road;
I contemplate the true mark of the body as it unfurls like a ram’s horn,
while the delusive karma of worldly attachments lies hidden like fish scales.
Therefore, it is like a poison that agitates a madman, or wine that awakens a drunkard;
it uncovers a treasury of true gold hidden beneath the grass of fatness,
and causes a general of vast learning to stand as still as one who is intoxicated.
Thus, all the guests from within the four seas are my people.
Now, the spirit of the ten armies is high, and the five generals are heroes.
Seizing this opportunity, I established the ancestral temples of the state.
Bowing my head in reverence, I ascended the throne and presided over the realm from the palace balcony, inheriting the kingly enterprise, grasping the charts of destiny,
and receiving the Mandate of Heaven.
This humble and frail wheel may serve as a worthy counterpart to the golden wheel;
its spirit exceeds that of a swift steed and shall suffice for the role of the dark-blue horse.
The robes and caps are no longer divided, and the chariots and books have already become one.
Now, may you fan the long wind within this burning house and grind the high carriages to dust at the gate.
He explained that he was donning his armor to begin anew with the people.
Both the general and his soldiers were devoid of strategic wisdom and had lost all their strength;
with no further path ahead and arrows exhausted, they abandoned their horses and set fire to their boats.
The mantis raising its arms is truly pitiable;
it is truly shameful.
When Robber Zhi led his troops to invade and plunder the feudal lords,
Kong Qiu set up battle formations and broke into a sweat while returning to his headquarters;
this was precisely what the clear instructions for a general prohibit.
When the Crown Prince Maitreya ascended the throne from his manor, I,
with my horses of sweat-stained merit returning to court,
came before the imperial palace bearing my transgressions.
General, you have summoned me;
I do not yet dare to accept your command.
My feelings run deep, yet my brush is short.
I cannot write at length;
I hope that you, O noble gentleman, will look beyond these words to our mutual expectations.
Pāpīyān bows his head in confession of his transgressions.

General Bo Tong, Great Officer Zhou Wudai,
Commander-in-Chief for the Coordination of All Military Affairs, and Overseer of the Royal Subjects, Zhi Xingyan,
respectfully submit this memorial: Your servant has heard that...
While governance was tranquil and the realm at peace,
ruffians occasionally rose up;
when transformation became pure, execution was abolished.
The rebellious faction took advantage of this situation to rise up.
Consequently, King Wenming led his hunt throughout the nine regions and encountered the Demon of Death at Mount Tu.
Mundianling caused his wheel to soar over the six realms;
he encountered greedy bandits in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Thus, when his body perished, it was known that his majestic spirit had dispersed to Min and Yue.
To have drifted to a foreign land and lost one’s honorable position is truly due to harboring treachery within while establishing worldly tracks without;
it is because rewards were granted based on false merit and punishments were inconsistent with the wickedness of ministers.
Since the Emperor Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One, passed away at Kuśinagara,
more than a millennium has swiftly elapsed.
The Crown Prince Maitreya Ajita now attends to his affairs in Tuṣita Heaven.
Lacking the means to carry on the succession,
the Citadel of Dharma was briefly left empty and the Wheel of Brahma had no master.
The realm of dust rebelled abroad, and the Sha-zhou region failed to offer tribute.
Consequently, the winds of the triple world were stirred and the beacon fires of the six heavens blazed up;
the heterodox followers with their deceptive doctrines inverted the customs,
while the false Lord of the Heavens, the sovereign king Pāpīyas, reigned as a usurper.
Innate nature clouded by suspicion and the body imbued with depraved influences,
arrogance dwells in the heart while the bonds of craving fill the mind;
he usurps the sacred life-force and illicitly manipulates the divine vessel.
They abandoned themselves to the desires of the realm of passion and peered covetously at the imperial domain.
Furthermore, their governance and teachings fell into decay as internal and external affairs became discordant;
sisters committed incest together, and the thousand sons divided in their loyalties.
The three daughters, licentious and wanton, invited me to their inner chambers;
before they could display their charms, I had already brought about my own old age.
Furthermore, Pāpīyān indulges in and practices the minor paths.
He possessed considerable talent and eloquence;
yet he was obstinate and refused counsel, glossed over his own faults, delighted in what was right, and was prone to fierce anger,
refusing to heed the words of his compliant son.
They exclusively followed the schemes of sycophantic ministers;
they waited for a rift in the state and took advantage of its vulnerabilities to launch an invasion,
falsely aligning themselves with the great generals, the various afflictions (*kleśa*), and others.
Because the momentum of the Noble Path has waned,
the eight hundred *ābhāsvara* gods and the ten *anantarya* fetters have arisen;
they have thus arrayed their armies of desire upon the ocean of craving.
He mistook the horse for a high plateau;
he held the reins within the realm of dualistic views and galloped through the domain of ignorance.
When encountering the Sage, he rolls up his traces and dwells in lofty seclusion;
when meeting with evil, he releases it within the central realm.
Bearing the weight of perilous barriers, he establishes himself by observing the times.
Some, seeking honor and profit, feign sleep at the gates of powerful families;
others harbor resentment toward the masses, specializing in the practice of poison and harm;
their arrogance is towering as they stubbornly cling to the Vaipulya sutras.
The remote borderlands of arrogance have not yet recognized our calendar;
we must now dispatch the seven envoys and their carriages,
and through the three obstacles, falsely proclaim the six articles of law to bring these alien customs under our influence.
The fool accepts the teaching and washes his collar;
the wise man rejects it and drinks from the mountain stream.
The soldiers wait for their rations ahead, while the beacon fires advance.
The false Four Heavenly Great Commanders, the Five Aggregates Maras,
and their ilk have established their dwellings at the source of beginninglessness and taken up residence within the realm of form.
They drift amidst the sea of suffering and wallow in negligence at the edge of the burning house;
they usurp titles for themselves and falsely assume the offices of the six ministries.
They plundered glory for a fleeting moment while indulging in pleasure for the time being.
Yet before long, the sovereign was gone and the corvée laborers were beyond counting;
hungry soldiers and envious troops flowed like rivers and spread across the fields.
Terrifying beings and grieving people fill the mountains and valleys;
those who share in evil seek one another out to form a confederacy in a single region,
while diverse classes gather in troops to station their armies throughout the three realms.
The false office of the Administration Commission (Xing Tai) has its own life and death;
the rebel Wang Guan stations his troops at the Five Paths and places his soldiers at the Three Sufferings.
Born into a realm that defies the mandate of Heaven, he grew old as a rebel.
As the five signs of decay announced their arrival, he responded to the world through the four modes of birth.
He dammed the source of the spring and extinguished the drifting flames.
The power of karma roars and surges,
leading the fragile and precarious to race ahead;
the three poisons falter and hesitate.
Embracing all that exists, they depart forever;
how can they endure such lack of kinship when calamity extends through the nine branches of their clan?
As both wrath and favor are exercised interchangeably, even the loyal and filial are subjected to execution.
Only then did they suddenly slander the sages, misrepresent the worthy, deceive the truth,
and subvert the upright; they laid traps for the common people and ensnared the masses,
recklessly claiming that which is suffering and empty as their own possession.
The momentum of this sudden shock was such that it was as solid as metal or stone.
At the hour of dusk on the thirtieth day of the first month.
There was a man surnamed Shan (Good) and named Zhishi (Knowledge).
Coming from the site of the Way, he announced:
"The thieves are not far from here."
"You should cut it down and suppress it immediately;
otherwise, it will become a great calamity.
When the minister heard these words, he did not yet fully believe them with reverence.
Driving a single sheep-cart, he turned the army toward the transformation-city;
he merely prepared his defenses by deeply digging moats and erecting palisades.
Just as the night was deepening, the enemy dispatched a messenger.
He has come with many rare and exotic tributes,
seeking to establish peace and friendship.
Your servant knows that this rebel's power is like a bubble or a flame.
No strategy could be devised.
His disposition was wild and violent, making him difficult to approach;
therefore, they did not speak with him.
Leaving with resentment,
he prepared many deceptive contrivances intending to invade and press upon us;
this was on the seventh day of the month.
At dawn, he emerges through the gateway of skillful means,
the place of sudden liberation;
he dispatches the postal couriers of faith to penetrate deeply and leads the multitude of the deluded out of the sea of suffering.
I have compiled these samādhis to establish a single moat,
hoping to sweep away the five aggregates and purify all realms of existence.
Yet the thieves still rely on the fortifications of a single river to resist the imperial majesty.
The waters overflowed, vast and deep beyond measure;
moreover, they encountered a swirling tempest that raged violently,
as hail and sleet poured down and crashing waves surged upward.
The Sea God finally surged forth seven kinds of diverse creatures,
some flying and others sinking;
yakṣas guarded the paths and rākṣasas occupied the fords.
The current blinds those who can see and deafens those who can hear, submerging the wealth of goodness;
those who wish to wade or swim across it rarely avoid drowning.
Furthermore, one stands on the brink of a precipice at the water's edge.
They constructed great fortifications with walls rising vertically and moats so deep they were perilous;
there was but a single gate.
Deep valleys hang down on all four sides;
a single man grasping a halberd causes ten thousand men to hold their thoughts in awe.
Those of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path are timid and daunted, while the pratyekabuddhas tremble with fear.
He then assembled the multitude and announced his plan to advance;
striking the drums with urgency,
they all agreed that it would be best to immediately order the soldiers to cross the river.
Therefore, we have prepared rafts by weaving various grasses and woods together;
you are instructed to cling to and step upon them to advance directly against the cross-currents, while we,
your subjects, shall manually press down upon the life-preserving bags.
He traveled upstream against the current,
steadfastly protecting himself without fail until he reached the other shore.
There, he divided his officers and soldiers and prepared his chariots and troops.
With single-minded resolve and united effort, they galloped forth to suppress [the rebels].
He immediately dispatched General Anjing to lead the troops of Guanlei.
Based on the source of the distraction,
he further commanded General Pacifier of Wrath to lead the vast and abundant forces.
He blocked the mouth of the Se-nu Valley and further commanded General Zhen-hui to lead the forces of Guangji.
Sever the path of stinginess and greed;
furthermore, command General Bōtōng to marshal the men of profound penetration.
He guarded the path against the mad and deluded.

The Chancellor of the Administration feared that the multitude might encounter one another and fail to advance in competition;
he therefore exhorted and spurred the six armies to establish them in the stage of *avaivartika*.
Yet, the lingering embers and wandering spirits sought refuge in the security of the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* heaven.
Leading forth dogs and sheep, they sought to come and resist in battle;
they merely feigned tigers and rhinoceroses to create an air of awe,
and summoned bears and leopards for their own protection.
